title: Hamilton Jacobi Equations and Viscosity Solutions

items.title: The Hamilton--Jacobi Cauchy problem and its classical solutions
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and open
([[def-metric-topology]]), let $T>0$, and let
$H:O\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]). Write
$$Z:=O\times(0,T),\qquad \overline Z:=\overline O\times[0,T],\qquad \Gamma:=(O\times\{0\})\cup(\partial O\times[0,T])$$
for the open space--time cylinder, its closure in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, and the
parabolic boundary. Given a continuous $u_0:O\to\mathbb R$, the
**Hamilton--Jacobi Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0\ \text{in }Z,\qquad u=u_0\ \text{on }O\times\{0\},$$
where $Du$ denotes the spatial gradient and $u_t$ the time derivative of the
unknown function ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
[[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]).

A **classical solution** of this problem is a function
$u\in C^0(\overline Z)\cap C^1(Z)$
([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]) with
$u(x,0)=u_0(x)$ for every $x\in O$ and
$$u_t(x,t)+H(x,t,Du(x,t))=0\qquad\text{for every }(x,t)\in Z .$$
The continuity requirement $u\in C^0(\overline Z)$ ensures continuous attainment of the initial datum and also continuity on
the lateral and terminal faces; no condition on the lateral face
$\partial O\times[0,T]$ is imposed unless it is stated explicitly.

**Stationary specialization.** Suppose that $H$ does not depend on $t$ and
that $v\in C^1(O)$ satisfies $H(x,Dv(x))=0$ for every $x\in O$; such a $v$ is
called a **classical solution of the stationary Hamilton--Jacobi equation**
$H(x,Dv)=0$. If in addition $v$ extends continuously to $\overline O$, then
$u(x,t):=v(x)$ is a classical solution of the Cauchy problem with datum
$u_0:=v|_O$, because $u\in C^0(\overline Z)\cap C^1(Z)$ and
$u_t\equiv0$ on $Z$.
items.strategy: Definition and notational contract; no proof. The item fixes (i) the open cylinder $Z=O\times(0,T)$, its closure and its parabolic boundary, (ii) the initial face $O\times\{0\}$ on which the datum is read, (iii) the Hamiltonian domain $O\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n$ and its continuity, and (iv) the regularity class $C^0(\overline Z)\cap C^1(Z)$ of a classical solution, so that 'the initial datum is attained' means continuous attainment and not a mere pointwise boundary value. The stationary specialization is recorded so that the later convex-duality section can refer to the stationary equation without redefining its solution class. No choice principle occurs. S: [TR] Chapter 1 (1.1)--(1.6), printed pp. 9--13, and Chapter 2 (2.15), printed p. 64; [CIL] (0.1)--(0.3) and Section 8, printed pp. 3--5 and 49--50.

items.title: Upper and lower semicontinuous envelopes by local limsup and liminf
items.statement:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty
([[def-metric-topology]]) and let $u:A\to\mathbb R$. For $x\in A$ and $r>0$
put
$$M_r(x):=\sup\{u(y):y\in A,\ |y-x|\le r\},\qquad m_r(x):=\inf\{u(y):y\in A,\ |y-x|\le r\},$$
the supremum and infimum being taken in
$\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

The **upper semicontinuous envelope** of $u$ is
$$u^*(x):=\inf_{r>0}M_r(x)=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\ \sup_{\substack{y\in A\\ |y-x|\le r}}u(y),$$
and the **lower semicontinuous envelope** of $u$ is
$$u_*(x):=\sup_{r>0}m_r(x)=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\ \inf_{\substack{y\in A\\ |y-x|\le r}}u(y),$$
both with values in $\overline{\mathbb R}$.
items.strategy: Definition and notational contract; no proof. The two envelopes are defined by monotone limits of the local supremum $M_r$ and local infimum $m_r$, so no regularity of $u$ enters and no choice is needed: the limits are the values of monotone sequences in $\overline{\mathbb R}$ indexed by $r=1/k$. Boundedness of $u$ is recorded as the hypothesis under which the envelopes are real-valued. S: [CIL] Section 4, the display preceding Theorem 4.1, printed p. 22; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 8, the definition of semicontinuous envelopes used in Perron's method, printed p. 33.

items.title: The envelopes are the least upper and greatest lower semicontinuous functions
items.statement:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty and let $u:A\to\mathbb R$ be bounded,
with envelopes $u^*,u_*$ as in
[[def-upper-and-lower-semicontinuous-envelopes]]. Then $u^*$ is upper
semicontinuous on $A$, $u_*$ is lower semicontinuous on $A$, and
$u_*\le u\le u^*$ pointwise. Moreover: (1) $u^*$ is the least upper
semicontinuous function $w:A\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ with $w\ge u$ pointwise,
and $u^*=u$ if and only if $u$ is upper semicontinuous; (2) $u_*$ is the
greatest lower semicontinuous function $w:A\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ with
$w\le u$ pointwise, and $u_*=u$ if and only if $u$ is lower semicontinuous;
(3) $(u^*)^*=u^*$ and $(u_*)_*=u_*$. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Upper semicontinuity of $u^*$: fix $x\in A$ and $\varepsilon>0$; by the definition of $u^*(x)$ as an infimum over $r$ there is $\rho>0$ with $M_\rho(x)\le u^*(x)+\varepsilon$, and every $z$ with $|z-x|<\rho$ satisfies $M_{\rho-|z-x|}(z)\le M_\rho(x)$, hence $u^*(z)\le u^*(x)+\varepsilon$ whenever $|z-x|$ is small: $u^*$ is upper semicontinuous (and $u\ge u_*$, $u\le u^*$ follow from $u(x)\le M_r(x)$ and $m_r(x)\le u(x)$). For (1): if $w$ is upper semicontinuous with $w\ge u$ then for every $z$ near $x$ one has $w(z)\ge u(z)$ and, passing to the local supremum against $w$'s own upper semicontinuity, $u^*(x)\le w(x)$; so $u^*\le w$ and $u^*$ is the least such majorant. Conversely, if $u$ is upper semicontinuous and $u^*>u$ at some $x$, choose $y_k\in A$ with $y_k\to x$ and $u(y_k)\to u^*(x)>u(x)$, contradicting $u(x)\ge\limsup_{y\to x}u(y)$; the proof for $u_*$ is the mirror image. Part (3) follows from (1) applied to the upper semicontinuous function $u^*$. The same computation shows along the way that the local-limsup envelope is itself upper semicontinuous, so no separate regularity hypothesis is needed. P: monotone localisation; the argument uses only the definitions and the least-majorant property, no compactness and no choice. S: [CIL] Section 4, the display before Theorem 4.1 and its use in the proof of Lemma 4.2, printed pp. 22--24; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 8, the upper-envelope computation in the proof of Lemma 1.25, printed pp. 33--34.

items.title: Viscosity subsolutions and supersolutions of a first-order equation and of the Cauchy problem
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be nonempty open with coordinates
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$, and let
$H:U\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A function $u:U\to\mathbb R$
that is upper semicontinuous on $U$
([[def-semicontinuity-on-euclidean-subsets]]) is a **viscosity subsolution**
of $u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ in $U$ if for every $\phi\in C^1(U)$
([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]) and every point
$z_0\in U$ at which $u-\phi$ has a local maximum,
$$\phi_t(z_0)+H(z_0,D\phi(z_0))\le0 .$$
A function $v:U\to\mathbb R$ that is lower semicontinuous on $U$ is a
**viscosity supersolution** if for every $\phi\in C^1(U)$ and every point
$z_0\in U$ at which $v-\phi$ has a local minimum,
$$\phi_t(z_0)+H(z_0,D\phi(z_0))\ge0 .$$
A **viscosity solution** of the equation in $U$ is a function that is both a
viscosity subsolution and a viscosity supersolution.

**Cauchy problem.** Let $Z=O\times(0,T)$ and
$H:O\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be as in
[[def-hamilton-jacobi-cauchy-problem]], and let $u_0:O\to\mathbb R$. A
**viscosity subsolution of the Cauchy problem** is an upper semicontinuous
$u:Z\to\mathbb R$ satisfying the subsolution inequality at every $z_0\in Z$
together with the relaxed initial condition
$$\limsup_{\substack{(y,s)\to(x,0)\\ s>0,\ y\in O}}u(y,s)\le u_0(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in O ;$$
a **viscosity supersolution** $v$ satisfies the supersolution inequality at
every $z_0\in Z$ together with
$$\liminf_{\substack{(y,s)\to(x,0)\\ s>0,\ y\in O}}v(y,s)\ge u_0(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in O .$$
A **viscosity solution of the Cauchy problem** is a function that is both a
subsolution and a supersolution of the Cauchy problem; a continuous solution
of the Cauchy problem satisfies the initial data pointwise, $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$
for every $x\in O$.
items.strategy: Definition and notational contract; no proof. Three points are fixed deliberately. First, the test is a local maximum of $u-\phi$ (equivalently $u$ is touched from above by $\phi$) for the subsolution and a local minimum for the supersolution; reversing the extremum reverses the direction of the inequality, which is exactly what makes the sign error visible (see [[cex-reversing-the-contact-extremum-reverses-the-viscosity-inequality]]). Second, the subsolution must be upper semicontinuous and the supersolution lower semicontinuous, because those are the classes in which the required maxima and minima of $u-\phi$ exist; no continuity of $u$ is assumed and no a.e. class is used. Third, the Cauchy initial condition is the relaxed limsup/liminf condition, which for continuous functions reduces to the pointwise equality $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$. S: [CIL] Definition 2.2, Remarks 2.3 and (8.1)--(8.4), printed pp. 10--11 and 49--50; [TR] Chapter 1 equations (1.4)--(1.6) and (1.10), printed pp. 15--22; [BHJ] Section 3, definitions of viscosity sub- and supersolution, printed pp. 10--12.

items.title: Strictification of a viscosity test function by a quartic perturbation
items.statement:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $v:U\to\mathbb R$, let
$\phi\in C^1(U)$, suppose $v-\phi$ has a local maximum at $z_0\in U$, and fix
$r>0$ with $\overline B(z_0,r)\subseteq U$ and
$v(z)-\phi(z)\le v(z_0)-\phi(z_0)$ for every $z\in\overline B(z_0,r)$. For
$\varepsilon>0$ define
$$\phi_\varepsilon(z):=\phi(z)+\varepsilon|z-z_0|^4 .$$
Then $\phi_\varepsilon\in C^1(U)$ agrees with $\phi$ to first order at the
contact,
$$\phi_\varepsilon(z_0)=\phi(z_0),\qquad D\phi_\varepsilon(z_0)=D\phi(z_0),$$
and $v-\phi_\varepsilon$ has a strict maximum over $\overline B(z_0,r)$ at
$z_0$:
$$v(z)-\phi_\varepsilon(z)<v(z_0)-\phi_\varepsilon(z_0)\qquad\text{for every }z\in\overline B(z_0,r)\setminus\{z_0\} .$$
The same statement with $\phi_\varepsilon:=\phi-\varepsilon|z-z_0|^4$
strictifies a local minimum contact of a test function, and the first jet at
the contact is again unchanged. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Direct computation. For $z\in\overline B(z_0,r)$ the local-maximum hypothesis gives $v(z)-\phi(z)\le v(z_0)-\phi(z_0)$, and the quartic term is nonnegative with $|z-z_0|^4=0$ only at $z=z_0$; hence $v(z)-\phi_\varepsilon(z)\le v(z_0)-\phi(z_0)-\varepsilon|z-z_0|^4$ with strict inequality for $z\ne z_0$, which is the claimed strict maximum (the compact ball is needed only to have the phrase 'strict maximum over $\overline B(z_0,r)$' well posed and is supplied by [[cor-euclidean-closed-balls-and-spheres-are-compact]] together with the extreme-value theorem for semicontinuous functions; the pointwise inequality itself needs only the hypothesis). The first jet at $z_0$ is unchanged because $z\mapsto|z-z_0|^4$ has value $0$ and gradient $0$ at $z_0$; the minimum case is the same computation with the signs reversed. This is the standard strictification device that lets every nonstrict contact be treated as a strict one without changing the jet, so the perturbation never affects the viscosity inequalities. P: an explicit perturbation whose first jet vanishes at the contact; no choice. S: [CIL] Section 2 and Theorem 3.2, the standard strict-contact reduction, printed pp. 11--17; [BHJ] Section 3, strict maxima in the subsolution test, printed pp. 10--12.

items.title: Discontinuous viscosity solutions through the two envelopes
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $T>0$, let
$H:O\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, $Z=O\times(0,T)$,
and let $u_0:O\to\mathbb R$. A locally bounded function $u:Z\to\mathbb R$ is a
**viscosity solution of the Cauchy problem** if its upper semicontinuous
envelope $u^*$ is a viscosity subsolution and its lower semicontinuous
envelope $u_*$ is a viscosity supersolution in the sense of
[[def-viscosity-subsolution-and-supersolution]], each carrying the initial
datum $u_0$ in the relaxed limsup/liminf sense. Both envelopes are taken over
$Z$ as a subset of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$
([[def-upper-and-lower-semicontinuous-envelopes]]); the subsolution
inequalities are imposed at every point of $Z$ and the relaxed initial
conditions at every point of $O$.

A **continuous viscosity solution** is a viscosity solution $u$ that is
continuous on $Z$. For such a $u$ one has $u^*=u_*=u$
(apply [[lem-envelopes-are-the-least-semicontinuous-majorants]] on a small
closed ball about each interior point, where continuity makes $u$ bounded).
The relaxed initial conditions give a continuous extension to the initial
face with value $u_0$, so the definition
specializes to the one for continuous test functions. In the opposite
direction, the envelope formulation is forced whenever $u$ is not continuous:
it keeps the subsolution inequality attached to $u^*$ and the supersolution
inequality to $u_*$, and never asks a single discontinuous function to satisfy
both.
items.strategy: Definition and notational contract; no proof. The point of the envelope formulation is that a merely locally bounded $u$ need not be upper or lower semicontinuous, so the equation cannot be imposed on $u$ directly; instead $u^*$ carries the subsolution condition and $u_*$ the supersolution condition, and $u$ is a solution exactly when both envelopes solve their respective one-sided problems. For continuous $u$ the two roles coincide. This is the definition used for the half-relaxed limits of the later stability theorems and for the comparison and Perron statements, where the objects produced by envelopes are not known to be continuous in advance. S: [CIL] Section 4 and the construction in the proof of Theorem 4.1, printed pp. 22--25; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 8 and Remark 1.31, printed pp. 33--37; [BHJ] Section 4, stability properties, printed pp. 12--14.

items.title: Viscosity testing by first-order jets, and closure of the jet inequality
items.statement:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open and let
$H:U\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. For $w:U\to\mathbb R$ and
$z_0\in U$ define the first-order superjet and subjet
$$D^+w(z_0):=\{p=(p_x,p_t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\ w(z)\le w(z_0)+\langle p,z-z_0\rangle+o(|z-z_0|)\ \ (z\to z_0)\},$$
$$D^-w(z_0):=-D^+(-w)(z_0)=\{p:\ w(z)\ge w(z_0)+\langle p,z-z_0\rangle+o(|z-z_0|)\ (z\to z_0)\}.$$
Then: (1) an upper semicontinuous $u:U\to\mathbb R$ is a viscosity subsolution
of $u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ in $U$ if and only if
$$p_t+H(z_0,p_x)\le0\qquad\text{for all }z_0\in U\text{ and all }p\in D^+u(z_0);$$
(2) a lower semicontinuous $v$ is a viscosity supersolution if and only if
$p_t+H(z_0,p_x)\ge0$ for all $z_0\in U$ and all $p\in D^-v(z_0)$; (3) if $u$
is such a subsolution, $z_k\to z_0$ in $U$ with $u(z_k)\to u(z_0)$, and
$p_k\in D^+u(z_k)$ with $p_k\to p$, then $p_t+H(z_0,p_x)\le0$; the analogous
closure statement holds for supersolutions and subjets. The closure statement
does not assert that $p$ itself belongs to $D^+u(z_0)$; that membership may
fail, and it is not needed. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Equivalence. Suppose p lies in the superjet of u at z₀. For small h, let r(h) be the positive part of u(z₀+h)−u(z₀)−⟨p,h⟩. The superjet condition says r(h)=o(|h|). Thus μ(s):=sup_{0<|h|≤s} r(h)/|h| tends to 0 as s↓0. Fix once and for all a smooth dyadic partition of unity χⱼ on 0<r<r₀, with χⱼ supported where 2^(−j−1)≤r≤2^(−j+1) and |χⱼ′|≤C2ʲ. Set aⱼ:=μ(2^(−j+2))+2^(−j) and θ(r):=r∑ⱼaⱼχⱼ(r), with θ(0)=0. Every annulus coefficient is defined by a supremum, so no sequence of choices is used. If χⱼ(r)≠0, then μ(r)≤μ(2^(−j+2))≤aⱼ; hence θ(r)≥rμ(r)≥r(h) whenever |h|=r. The dyadic derivative bound and aⱼ→0 give θ′(r)→0, while θ(r)/r→0, so h↦θ(|h|) is C¹ at 0 with derivative 0. Therefore φ(z₀+h):=u(z₀)+⟨p,h⟩+θ(|h|) is C¹, has derivative p at z₀, and is an upper test for u there. The viscosity inequality gives p_t+H(z₀,p_x)≤0. This smooth majorant is essential: a fixed quadratic need not dominate an arbitrary o(|h|) remainder. Conversely, if u−φ has a local maximum at z₀, differentiability of φ gives Dφ(z₀) in the superjet directly. The subjet equivalence is the same argument applied to −v. For the closure assertion, apply the jet inequality at z_k and pass to the limit using z_k→z₀, p_k→p, u(z_k)→u(z₀), and continuity of H; this is the closure-of-the-inequality statement, and does not assert p is in the superjet at z₀. P: a deterministic dyadic smooth majorant of the vanishing first-order remainder, followed by continuity for closure. S: [CIL] (2.1)–(2.7), Definition 2.2, Remark 2.4 and the exercise after Remark 2.3, printed pp. 9–12; [TR] Chapter 1 Sections 1–2, one-sided differentials D±, printed pp. 15–18; [BHJ] Section 2, one-sided differentials, printed pp. 6–9.

items.title: Classical solutions are viscosity solutions and differentiable viscosity solutions solve the equation pointwise
items.statement:
Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $T>0$, let
$H:O\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, let
$u_0:O\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $Z=O\times(0,T)$.
(1) If $u\in C^1(Z)\cap C^0(\overline Z)$ satisfies
$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ pointwise on $Z$ and $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$ on $O$ (a classical
solution in the sense of [[def-hamilton-jacobi-cauchy-problem]]), then $u$ is a
viscosity solution of the Cauchy problem. (2) Conversely, if $u:Z\to\mathbb R$
is a continuous viscosity solution and $u$ is differentiable at a point
$z_0\in Z$, then
$$u_t(z_0)+H(z_0,Du(z_0))=0 .$$
In particular, a viscosity solution of class $C^1(Z)$ is a classical solution
of the equation on $Z$ (its initial trace being part of the Cauchy-problem
notion). No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: (1) If u is C¹ and solves the equation pointwise, then at a local maximum of u−φ Fermat’s theorem gives Dφ=Du, so the subsolution test is the pointwise equation; the supersolution case is identical at a local minimum. The initial trace is the one in [[def-hamilton-jacobi-cauchy-problem]]. (2) If u is differentiable at z₀, differentiability gives u(z₀+h)−u(z₀)−⟨Du(z₀),h⟩=o(|h|). Hence Du(z₀) belongs to both first-order jets by their definitions. Apply the two equivalences in [[lem-viscosity-testing-by-first-order-jets]] to obtain both opposite viscosity inequalities. This proves the pointwise equation without claiming that a fixed |h|² term dominates an arbitrary o(|h|) remainder. P: Fermat for a C¹ contact and the jet characterization for a merely differentiable function. S: [TR] Exercise 5 and Lemma 1.11, printed pp. 18–21; [CIL] Remark 2.3 and the discussion after Definition 2.2, printed pp. 10–11; [BHJ] Section 3, consistency of viscosity and classical solutions, printed pp. 10–12.

items.title: Finite maxima of subsolutions and finite minima of supersolutions
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open, and let
$H:U\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous.
(1) If $u_1,\dots,u_k$ are viscosity subsolutions of
$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ in $U$, then $u:=\max(u_1,\dots,u_k)$ is a viscosity
subsolution in $U$. (2) If $v_1,\dots,v_k$ are viscosity supersolutions, then
$v:=\min(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ is a viscosity supersolution in $U$. (3) For the
Cauchy problem on $Z=O\times(0,T)$ the same statements hold when all the
functions carry the same continuous initial datum $u_0$ in the relaxed sense;
the maximum of subsolutions then also satisfies the relaxed initial condition
for $u_0$. The mixed operations are not asserted: a finite minimum of
subsolutions and a finite maximum of supersolutions need not preserve the
corresponding inequality when the equation has a zero-order term.
No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: At a local maximum point $z_0$ of $u-\phi$ choose an index $i$ with $u_i(z_0)=u(z_0)$ (possible because the maximum of finitely many reals is attained at some index, [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). Since $u_i\le u$ pointwise, for $z$ near $z_0$ we have $u_i(z)-\phi(z)\le u(z)-\phi(z)\le u(z_0)-\phi(z_0)=u_i(z_0)-\phi(z_0)$, so $u_i-\phi$ also has a local maximum at $z_0$; the subsolution inequality for $u_i$ gives $\phi_t(z_0)+H(z_0,D\phi(z_0))\le0$, which is the required inequality for $u$. The supersolution statement is the mirror image with minima. The initial conditions are preserved because each $u_i$ satisfies $\limsup u_i\le u_0$ and a finite maximum of limsups is the limsup of the maximum. The mixed cases genuinely fail without the same index argument, and the example on the companion page shows the failure for a proper equation; no envelope or supremum over an infinite family is asserted here. P: select the active index at the contact; no choice beyond the finite selection of an index. S: [CIL] Proposition 4.1(1) and the remarks preceding Lemma 4.2, printed pp. 22--23; [TR] Chapter 1 Lemma 1.25 and its discussion of the finite case, printed pp. 33--34; [BHJ] Section 4, stability under finite maxima, printed pp. 12--14.

items.title: Stability of viscosity sub-, super- and solutions under locally uniform convergence
items.statement:
Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $T>0$, $Z=O\times(0,T)$, and
$Z_0=O\times[0,T)$. Let
$H_k,H:O\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with
$H_k\to H$ uniformly on every compact subset as $k\to\infty$. For each $k$,
let $u_k:Z_0\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u_k$ restricted to $Z$ a
viscosity subsolution of $(u_k)_t+H_k(x,t,Du_k)=0$ and with
$u_k(x,0)=u_0^{(k)}(x)$. Suppose $u_0^{(k)}\to u_0$ locally uniformly on $O$
and $u_k\to u$ locally uniformly on $Z_0$. Then $u$ is a viscosity subsolution
of $u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ in $Z$ and its continuous initial trace is $u_0$. The
same statement holds for supersolutions, and combining the two, locally
uniform limits of viscosity solutions are viscosity solutions. The conclusion
is insensitive to the sign of the approximation: no differentiability and no
monotonicity of convergence is used, only local uniformity up to the initial
face. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: For the interior equation, fix φ∈C¹(Z) and a strict local maximum of u−φ at z₀; strictify without changing Dφ(z₀) using [[lem-strictification-of-a-viscosity-test-function-by-a-quartic-perturbation]]. Choose a closed ball around z₀ contained in Z. Local uniform convergence on that compact ball makes u_k−φ attain maxima at points z_k that converge to z₀; the maximum values converge to u(z₀)−φ(z₀). The subsolution inequality for u_k at z_k is φ_t(z_k)+H_k(z_k,Dφ(z_k))≤0. Pass to the limit using compact-uniform convergence of H_k and continuity of φ and H to obtain φ_t(z₀)+H(z₀,Dφ(z₀))≤0. For the initial trace, local uniform convergence on compact subsets of Z₀ includes t=0, so u(x,0)=lim_k u_k(x,0)=lim_k u₀^(k)(x)=u₀(x) locally uniformly; the relaxed initial condition follows. The same proof with lower contacts gives the supersolution result. Interior convergence on Z alone does not imply this boundary conclusion; convergence up to t=0 is the stated hypothesis. P: compact maximum localisation and passage to the limit in the test inequality. S: [TR] Theorem 1.13 and its proof, printed pp. 21–22; [CIL] Section 4, stability of viscosity solutions, printed pp. 22–23; [BHJ] Section 4, stability, printed pp. 12–14.

items.title: Half-relaxed limits of a locally bounded family
items.statement:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open ([[def-metric-topology]]) and let
$(u_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon\in(0,1)}$ be a family of real-valued functions on
$U$ that is **locally bounded**: for every compact $K\subseteq U$ there is
$M_K<\infty$ with $|u_\varepsilon(y)|\le M_K$ for all $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$
and $y\in K$. The **upper half-relaxed limit** and the **lower half-relaxed
limit** of the family, computed in $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-epsilon]]), are
$$\overline u(z):=\limsup_{\substack{\varepsilon\downarrow0\\ U\ni y\to z}}u_\varepsilon(y):=\inf_{\delta>0}\ \sup\bigl\{u_\varepsilon(y):0<\varepsilon<\delta,\ y\in U,\ |y-z|<\delta\bigr\},$$
$$\underline u(z):=\liminf_{\substack{\varepsilon\downarrow0\\ U\ni y\to z}}u_\varepsilon(y):=\sup_{\delta>0}\ \inf\bigl\{u_\varepsilon(y):0<\varepsilon<\delta,\ y\in U,\ |y-z|<\delta\bigr\}.$$
The quantifiers range over the index $\varepsilon$ and the point $y$
simultaneously, so the limit records the behaviour of the whole family near
$z$, not the limit of the single family of values $(u_\varepsilon(z))_{\varepsilon}$;
both envelopes are local and depend only on the germ of the family at $z$.
items.strategy: Definition and notational contract; no proof. The definition makes the two features required by the stability theorems explicit. First, the limsup is over the pair $(\varepsilon,y)$ with both quantifiers active, so a value $L$ with $L>\underline u(z)$ must be approached by an actual sequence $(\varepsilon_j,y_j)\to(0,z)$; this is what makes the half-relaxed limit the correct tool when the family is only locally bounded. Second, the envelopes are computed without selecting a sequence of indices, so no countable or dependent choice is used, in contrast with subsequential compactness arguments (the plan's choice ledger records this distinction for PDE-25). Upper semicontinuity of $\overline u$ is the same monotone-localisation computation as in [[lem-envelopes-are-the-least-semicontinuous-majorants]] applied to the family indexed by $\delta$. S: [CIL] Section 6 and the limit notions used in Theorem 6.2, printed pp. 38--40; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 4, the locally uniform stability statement, printed pp. 21--22; [BHJ] Section 4, limits of viscosity solutions, printed pp. 12--14.

items.title: Half-relaxed limits of sub- and supersolutions with vanishing perturbations
items.statement:
Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $T>0$, $Z=O\times(0,T)$, let
$H_\varepsilon,H:O\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous for
$\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, and let $(u_\varepsilon)$ be a locally bounded family of
real functions on $Z$ that are upper semicontinuous in the subsolution case.
Assume one of the two forms of the Hamiltonian condition: (a)
$H_\varepsilon\to H$ uniformly on compact subsets of
$O\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n$; or (b) the exact limit-inferior condition:
for all sequences $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$, $z_j\to z\in Z$ and
$p_j\to p$ one has $\liminf_jH_{\varepsilon_j}(z_j,p_j)\ge H(z,p)$. Suppose
moreover that for every $\phi\in C^1(Z)$ and every local maximum point
$z_\varepsilon\in Z$ of $u_\varepsilon-\phi$ there holds
$$\phi_t(z_\varepsilon)+H_\varepsilon(z_\varepsilon,D\phi(z_\varepsilon))\le c_\varepsilon(z_\varepsilon),$$
where $c_\varepsilon:Z\to[0,\infty)$ is locally bounded with
$c_\varepsilon\to0$ locally uniformly. Then the upper half-relaxed limit
$\overline u$ ([[def-half-relaxed-limits]]) is a viscosity subsolution of
$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ in $Z$. If in addition
$u_\varepsilon(x,0)\le u_0^{(\varepsilon)}(x)$ in the relaxed sense with
$u_0^{(\varepsilon)}\to u_0$ locally uniformly on $O$ and the family is locally
equicontinuous up to the initial face, then $\overline u$ carries the initial
datum $u_0$ in the relaxed sense. The dual statement with $\limsup_jH_{\varepsilon_j}(z_j,p_j)\le H(z,p)$,
$\ge-c_\varepsilon$ and the lower half-relaxed limit holds for supersolutions.
**Choice.** Under hypothesis (a) the proof is choice-free. Under hypothesis
(b) it extracts a sequence of near-maximisers at the relaxed limit and
therefore uses Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is declared
as a dependency; the extraction is the only place where the principle is
consumed.
items.strategy: Fix $\phi\in C^1(Z)$ and a strict local maximum of $\overline u-\phi$ at $z_0$; strictness is arranged by [[lem-strictification-of-a-viscosity-test-function-by-a-quartic-perturbation]]. By the definition of the upper half-relaxed limit and of a strict local maximum there are sequences $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$, $y_j\to z_0$ with $u_{\varepsilon_j}(y_j)\to\overline u(z_0)$. For each $j$ choose a maximum point $z_j$ of $u_{\varepsilon_j}-\phi$ on a fixed closed ball $\overline B(z_0,r)$; the same localisation as in [[thm-stability-of-viscosity-solutions-under-local-uniform-convergence]] gives $z_j\to z_0$ and $u_{\varepsilon_j}(z_j)\to\overline u(z_0)$ (lower bound from the competitor $y_j$, upper bound from the definition of the relaxed limit). The assumed inequality at $z_j$ gives $\phi_t(z_j)+H_{\varepsilon_j}(z_j,D\phi(z_j))\le c_{\varepsilon_j}(z_j)$ with $c_{\varepsilon_j}(z_j)\to0$; passing to the limit under condition (b), which is implied by (a), yields $\phi_t(z_0)+H(z_0,D\phi(z_0))\le0$. The initial condition follows by the same argument at the initial face, where local equicontinuity upgrades the relaxed limsup of a near sequence into the limsup of the data $u_0^{(\varepsilon)}$. The vanishing perturbation $c_\varepsilon$ is what the vanishing-viscosity theorem needs; no subsequence is selected and no choice principle is used. P: contact localisation for the relaxed envelope, then passage to the limit. S: [CIL] Section 6, Theorems 6.1--6.2 and their proofs, printed pp. 38--42; [BHJ] Section 4, stability and limits, printed pp. 12--14; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 4, printed pp. 21--22.

items.title: Doubling variables: existence, relative contacts at the maximiser and localisation
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, let $u:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded
above and upper semicontinuous, and let $v:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$
be bounded below and lower semicontinuous. Fix $\alpha,\rho>0$ and define
$$\Phi(x,y,t,s):=u(x,t)-v(y,s)-\frac{\alpha}{2}|x-y|^2-\frac{\alpha}{2}|t-s|^2-\rho\,(|x|^2+|y|^2)$$
on $\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]^2$, with
$M_{\alpha,\rho}:=\sup\Phi$. Then: (1) $M_{\alpha,\rho}$ is finite and
attained, and at every maximiser $(x_\alpha,y_\alpha,t_\alpha,s_\alpha)$ the
$C^1$ test functions
$$\psi_1(x,t):=\frac{\alpha}{2}|x-y_\alpha|^2+\frac{\alpha}{2}|t-s_\alpha|^2+\rho|x|^2,\qquad \psi_2(y,s):=-\frac{\alpha}{2}|x_\alpha-y|^2-\frac{\alpha}{2}|t_\alpha-s|^2-\rho|y|^2$$
satisfy: $u-\psi_1$ has a local maximum at $(x_\alpha,t_\alpha)$ and
$v-\psi_2$ has a local minimum at $(y_\alpha,s_\alpha)$, with
$$p_\alpha:=D_x\psi_1(x_\alpha)=\alpha(x_\alpha-y_\alpha)+2\rho x_\alpha,\qquad q_\alpha:=D_y\psi_2(y_\alpha)=\alpha(x_\alpha-y_\alpha)-2\rho y_\alpha,\qquad p^0_\alpha:=\partial_t\psi_1(t_\alpha)=\partial_s\psi_2(s_\alpha)=\alpha(t_\alpha-s_\alpha);$$
(2) for each fixed $\rho>0$, along any sequence of maximisers as
$\alpha\to\infty$,
$$\alpha\bigl(|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|^2+|t_\alpha-s_\alpha|^2\bigr)\longrightarrow0,\qquad (1+|p_\alpha|)\bigl(|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|+|t_\alpha-s_\alpha|\bigr)\longrightarrow0,\qquad |x_\alpha-y_\alpha|+|t_\alpha-s_\alpha|\longrightarrow0,$$
while $|q_\alpha-p_\alpha|=2\rho|x_\alpha+y_\alpha|$ is bounded by
$2\rho(|x_\alpha|+|y_\alpha|)$ and is not claimed to vanish for fixed $\rho$;
(3) at every maximiser
$$\frac{\alpha}{2}\bigl(|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|^2+|t_\alpha-s_\alpha|^2\bigr)+\rho\bigl(|x_\alpha|^2+|y_\alpha|^2\bigr)\le\sup u-\inf v-M_{\alpha,\rho},$$
so whenever the maximiser values $M_{\alpha,\rho}$ are bounded below by $m$ on
a set of parameters, the corresponding maximisers satisfy
$\rho(|x_\alpha|^2+|y_\alpha|^2)\le\sup u-\inf v-m$ and
$|q_\alpha-p_\alpha|\le2\bigl(2\rho(\sup u-\inf v-m)\bigr)^{1/2}$. No choice
principle is used.
items.strategy: Existence: $\Phi$ is upper semicontinuous and bounded above by $\sup u-\inf v<\infty$; the weight $-\rho(|x|^2+|y|^2)$ tends to $-\infty$ as $|x|+|y|\to\infty$, so the nonempty superlevel set $\{\Phi\ge\Phi(x_0,y_0,t_0,s_0)\}$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^{2n}\times[0,T]^2$, hence compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and an upper semicontinuous function attains its maximum on a nonempty compact set ([[thm-semicontinuous-evt]]). Contacts and gradients: fixing $y=y_\alpha$, $s=s_\alpha$ and using that $\Phi$ is maximal gives $u(x,t)-\psi_1(x,t)\le u(x_\alpha,t_\alpha)-\psi_1(x_\alpha,t_\alpha)$ for all $(x,t)$ (the terms in $y_\alpha,s_\alpha$ cancel), so $u-\psi_1$ has a local maximum at $(x_\alpha,t_\alpha)$; the mirror computation with $(x_\alpha,t_\alpha)$ fixed gives that $v-\psi_2$ has a local minimum at $(y_\alpha,s_\alpha)$. The displayed $p_\alpha,q_\alpha,p^0_\alpha$ are the derivatives of $\psi_1,\psi_2$ at the contacts. Localisation: $M_{\alpha,\rho}$ is nonincreasing in $\alpha$ and bounded below by $\Phi(0,0,0,0)$, hence converges, and evaluating $\Phi$ with the coefficient $\alpha/2$ at a maximiser of $\Phi$ gives $\frac{\alpha}{4}(|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|^2+|t_\alpha-s_\alpha|^2)\le M_{\alpha/2,\rho}-M_{\alpha,\rho}\to0$; the remaining estimates follow: $|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|+|t_\alpha-s_\alpha|\to0$, and with $|p_\alpha|\le\alpha|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|+2\rho|x_\alpha|$ and $x_\alpha$ bounded by (3), $(1+|p_\alpha|)|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|\le|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|+\alpha|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|^2+2\rho|x_\alpha||x_\alpha-y_\alpha|\to0$, while $|p_\alpha||t_\alpha-s_\alpha|\le\frac{\alpha}{2}(|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|^2+|t_\alpha-s_\alpha|^2)+2\rho|x_\alpha||t_\alpha-s_\alpha|\to0$. Weight bound: from the definition of $M_{\alpha,\rho}$ and $u(x_\alpha,t_\alpha)\le\sup u$, $-v(y_\alpha,s_\alpha)\le-\inf v$, the total penalty is $u(x_\alpha,t_\alpha)-v(y_\alpha,s_\alpha)-M_{\alpha,\rho}\le\sup u-\inf v-M_{\alpha,\rho}$, which is (3) and gives the stated corollaries for the ball radius and for $q_\alpha-p_\alpha=2\rho(x_\alpha+y_\alpha)$. The two viscosity inequalities used by the comparison theorem are then obtained by applying the sub- and supersolution definitions to the contacts $\psi_1,\psi_2$, with strictness supplied by the terminal-time penalisation of [[lem-time-penalisation-moves-a-doubling-variables-maximum-away-from-the-terminal-boundary]]. P: coercive weight for existence, monotonicity in $\alpha$ for localisation, and explicit $C^1$ contacts for the two tests. S: [CIL] Proposition 3.7 and Lemma 3.1, printed pp. 15--16 and 20--21, together with the parabolic doubling (8.8)--(8.10), printed pp. 51--52; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 6, Steps 1--2 of the proof of Theorem 1.19, printed pp. 27--28.

items.title: Time penalisation moves a doubling-variables maximum away from the terminal boundary
items.statement:
Let $T>0$, $Z=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$, and let
$H:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Suppose
$u,v:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R$, where $u$ is upper semicontinuous
and bounded above, $v$ is lower semicontinuous and bounded below, and their
restrictions to $Z$ are respectively a viscosity subsolution and a viscosity
supersolution of $u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$. For $\eta,\eta'>0$ put
$\tilde u_\eta(x,t)=u(x,t)-\eta/(T-t)$ and
$\tilde v_{\eta'}(x,t)=v(x,t)+\eta'/(T-t)$ for $t<T$. Then:
(1) every $C^1$ upper contact $\phi$ for $\tilde u_\eta$ at
$z_0=(x_0,t_0)\in Z$ satisfies
$$\phi_t(z_0)+H(x_0,t_0,D\phi(z_0))\le-\frac{\eta}{(T-t_0)^2}<0 ;$$
(2) every $C^1$ lower contact $\phi$ for $\tilde v_{\eta'}$ at $z_0\in Z$
satisfies
$$\phi_t(z_0)+H(x_0,t_0,D\phi(z_0))\ge\frac{\eta'}{(T-t_0)^2}>0 ;$$
moreover $\tilde u_\eta\to-\infty$ and $\tilde v_{\eta'}\to+\infty$ uniformly
in $x$ as $t\uparrow T$; (3) for every $\alpha,\rho>0$, define on
$\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]^2$
$$\Phi_{\alpha,\rho}(x,y,t,s)=\tilde u_\eta(x,t)-\tilde v_{\eta'}(y,s)-\frac{\alpha}{2}|x-y|^2-\frac{\alpha}{2}|t-s|^2-\rho(|x|^2+|y|^2)$$
when $t,s<T$, and set $\Phi_{\alpha,\rho}=-\infty$ when $t=T$ or $s=T$. Then
$\Phi_{\alpha,\rho}$ attains a finite maximum, and every maximiser has
$t,s<T$. A maximum may occur on an initial face (that is, with $t=0$ or
$s=0$). No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
For (1), if $\tilde u_\eta-\phi$ has a local maximum at $z_0$, then $u-(\phi+\eta/(T-t))$ has a local maximum there. The subsolution inequality for $u$, applied to this $C^1$ test, gives $\phi_t(z_0)+\eta/(T-t_0)^2+H(x_0,t_0,D\phi(z_0))\le0$. For (2), if $\tilde v_{\eta'}-\phi$ has a local minimum, then $v-(\phi-\eta'/(T-t))$ has a local minimum. Its time derivative is $\phi_t-\eta'/(T-t)^2$, so the supersolution inequality gives $\phi_t+H\ge\eta'/(T-t_0)^2$. The uniform terminal limits follow from $u\le\sup u$ and $v\ge\inf v$.
For (3), $\Phi_{\alpha,\rho}$ is upper semicontinuous on the closed time slab: at $t=0$ and $s=0$ this follows from the assumed semicontinuity of $u$ and $v$, and at a terminal face its value tends uniformly to $-\infty$ by the bounds and the two time penalties. It is bounded above by $\sup u-\inf v-\rho(|x|^2+|y|^2)$. Its value at any fixed diagonal point $(x,x,t,t)$ with $0<t<T$ is finite, so a nonempty superlevel set above a finite level is bounded in $(x,y)$, closed, and stays away from the terminal faces. Heine--Borel makes this set compact. The supremum of $\Phi_{\alpha,\rho}$ on it is finite; its closed superlevel sets approaching that supremum have the finite-intersection property, so compactness gives a common point where the supremum is attained. The level is chosen below the fixed finite diagonal value, hence this is also a global maximum. The terminal faces carry value $-\infty$, so no maximizer lies there. P: add the two explicit time-boundary penalties, then use spatial coercivity and compact superlevel sets. S: [CIL] proof of Theorem 8.2, the modification $\tilde u=u-\varepsilon/(T-t)$ and the dual penalty, printed p. 51; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 6, the time penalisation in the comparison proof, printed pp. 26--28.

items.title: Comparison for first-order Hamilton--Jacobi equations
items.statement:
Comparison for first-order Hamilton--Jacobi equations, in the two settings of
the design. **(a) The case $O=\mathbb R^n$.** Let $T>0$ and let
$H:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous for which
there is $C>0$ with
$$|H(x,t,p)-H(y,s,p)|\le C(1+|p|)\,(|x-y|+|t-s|),\qquad |H(x,t,p)-H(x,t,q)|\le C|p-q|$$
for all $x,y,p,q\in\mathbb R^n$ and $t,s\in[0,T]$. Let $u$ be a bounded upper
semicontinuous viscosity subsolution and $v$ a bounded lower semicontinuous
viscosity supersolution of the Cauchy problem in $Z=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$,
each defined on the closed slab $\mathbb R^n\times[0,T)$ and satisfying the
pointwise initial inequality $u(x,0)\le v(x,0)$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$.
Then $u\le v$ on $Z$. **(b) The compact-cylinder case.** Let
$O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be bounded and open, $T>0$, and let
$H:\overline O\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and
uniformly continuous in $(x,t)$ uniformly on bounded $p$-sets: there is a
nondecreasing modulus $\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\omega(0+)=0$ such
that
$$|H(x,t,p)-H(y,s,p)|\le\omega\bigl((1+|p|)\,(|x-y|+|t-s|)\bigr)$$
for all $(x,t),(y,s)\in\overline O\times[0,T]$ and all $p\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$u,v$ be continuous on $\overline Z=\overline O\times[0,T]$, $u$ a viscosity
subsolution and $v$ a viscosity supersolution of $u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ in $Z$,
with $u\le v$ on the parabolic boundary
$\Gamma=(O\times\{0\})\cup(\partial O\times[0,T])$. Then $u\le v$ on
$\overline Z$. No growth hypothesis on $H$ in the momentum variable is imposed
in this case; the modulus condition replaces it. For an $x$-independent
autonomous Hamiltonian $H(p)$, it holds with the zero modulus. No choice
principle is used.
items.strategy: Assume u>v somewhere and apply the strict terminal-time penalties. In both cases, if d²=|x-y|²+|t-s|² at a maximiser, comparing the α- and α/2-penalties gives αd²≤4(M_{α/2}-M_α); monotonicity and boundedness of M_α make ΔM:=M_{α/2}-M_α→0, and δ_α:=sqrt(4ΔM/α) bounds d. In case (a), the spatial weight confines every maximiser for fixed ρ, so |q-p|≤4ρC_ρ and 2(1+|p|)d≤2δ_α+8ΔM+4ρC_ρδ_α→0, which controls the required L1 space-time distance. Upper/lower semicontinuity and the initial order exclude the initial faces uniformly by compactness; subtracting the strict contact inequalities then gives B/T²≤4C sqrt(ρK_ρ)+o_α(1). Let α→∞ and then ρ↓0 for a contradiction. In case (b), the compact cylinder and common modulus of u,v exclude the initial and lateral faces. Here p=q and 2(1+|p|)d≤2δ_α+8ΔM→0, so the modulus condition gives B/T²≤ω(2δ_α+8ΔM)→0, a contradiction. All estimates hold for every maximiser, and the compact superlevel-set/FIP arguments select none. P: strict time penalties, uniform doubling-maximum localisation, and subtraction of viscosity inequalities. items.title: Uniqueness and sup-norm contraction for the Cauchy problem
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, and let
$H:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ satisfy the Lipschitz
conditions of part (a) of
[[thm-comparison-for-first-order-hamilton-jacobi-equations]]. (1) If $u,v$ are
bounded viscosity solutions of the Cauchy problem in
$Z=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$ with the same bounded continuous initial datum
$u_0$, then $u=v$ on $Z$; in particular the classical and the Hopf--Lax
solutions of later sections are the unique ones in the bounded class whenever
$H$ satisfies those conditions. (2) More generally, if $u,v$ are bounded
viscosity solutions with initial data $u_0,v_0$, then for every $T>0$
$$\sup_{z\in Z}(u-v)\le\max\Bigl(0,\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}(u_0(x)-v_0(x))\Bigr),$$
and applying the same bound to $v-u$ gives
$\sup_Z|u-v|\le\sup_{\mathbb R^n}|u_0-v_0|$ when the initial difference is
bounded. In particular the solution operator is a contraction in the supremum
norm on the bounded initial data. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: For uniqueness, use the envelope formulation of discontinuous viscosity solutions: the upper envelope of u is a bounded upper semicontinuous subsolution and the lower envelope of v is a bounded lower semicontinuous supersolution, both with the corresponding relaxed initial inequalities. Extend them at t=0 by their continuous data; the relaxed inequalities make the extensions semicontinuous on the closed slab, so comparison gives u*≤v_*. Since u≤u* and v_*≤v, this yields u≤v; exchanging u and v gives uniqueness and forces all envelopes to coincide. For general data, shift v by K=max(0,sup(u0-v0)); its lower envelope shifts by K, so comparison gives u*≤v_*+K and hence u-v≤K. Applying the same argument in the reverse order gives the sup-norm contraction. P: comparison applied to the semicontinuous envelopes, plus constant-shift invariance. S: [TR] Chapter 1 Corollary 1.20 and Section 6, printed pp. 26--29; [CIL] Section 5.B, stability with respect to data and the equation, printed pp. 34--36; [BHJ] Section 5, uniqueness consequences of comparison, printed pp. 14--20.

items.title: The upper envelope of a locally bounded supremum of subsolutions is a subsolution
items.statement:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open, let
$H:U\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $\mathcal F$ be a
nonempty family of real-valued upper semicontinuous viscosity subsolutions of
$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ in $U$. Put $w(z):=\sup_{w'\in\mathcal F}w'(z)$ for $z\in U$
and assume that $w$ is locally bounded above: $w(z)<\infty$ for every $z\in U$
and $w$ is bounded above on every compact subset of $U$. Then the upper
semicontinuous envelope $w^*$
([[def-upper-and-lower-semicontinuous-envelopes]]) is a viscosity subsolution
of $u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ in $U$. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Let $\phi\in C^1(U)$ and let $w^*-\phi$ have a local maximum at $z_0$; strictify it with [[lem-strictification-of-a-viscosity-test-function-by-a-quartic-perturbation]] and fix a closed ball $\overline B(z_0,r)\subseteq U$ on which the strict maximum is attained at $z_0$. From the definition of $w^*$ as the envelope of the supremum there are $w_j\in\mathcal F$ and points $y_j\to z_0$ with $w_j(y_j)\to w^*(z_0)$ (take a sequence approaching the supremum at points near $z_0$ and pass to the limit using local boundedness). For each $j$ let $z_j$ be a point of $\overline B(z_0,r)$ maximising $w_j-\psi$ with $\psi:=\phi+2\delta|z-z_0|^2$, $\delta>0$ fixed; such a point exists because $w_j-\psi$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact ball. Comparing with the competitor $y_j$ gives $\liminf_j w_j(z_j)\ge w^*(z_0)$, while the defining property of the envelope and the strict contact at $z_0$ give $\limsup_j w_j(z_j)\le w^*(z_0)$; hence $z_j\to z_0$ and $w_j(z_j)\to w^*(z_0)$. Since $z_j$ is a maximum of $w_j-\psi$, we have $D\psi(z_j)\in D^+w_j(z_j)$, so the subsolution inequality for $w_j$ reads $\psi_t(z_j)+H(z_j,D\psi(z_j))\le0$; passing to the limit and then letting $\delta\downarrow0$ turns $D\psi(z_j)=D\phi(z_j)+4\delta(z_j-z_0)$ into $D\phi(z_0)$ and gives $\phi_t(z_0)+H(z_0,D\phi(z_0))\le0$. This is the load-bearing half of Perron's method; it uses no choice because the near-maximisers are selected by an explicit maximisation over a compact set, not by an axiom. P: near-maximiser selection plus strict test perturbation. S: [CIL] Lemma 4.2 and Proposition 4.3, printed pp. 23--24; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 8, Lemma 1.25 and its upper-envelope discussion, printed pp. 33--34.

items.title: Failure of the supersolution test for the lower envelope allows a local bump
items.statement:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open, let
$H:U\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $w:U\to\mathbb R$ be
an upper semicontinuous viscosity subsolution of $u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ in $U$.
Suppose the lower semicontinuous envelope $w_*$ fails the supersolution test
at $\hat z\in U$ in the following precise sense: $w_*(\hat z)\in\mathbb R$ and there is $\phi\in C^1(U)$ such that
$w_*-\phi$ has a local minimum at $\hat z$ and
$$\phi_t(\hat z)+H(\hat z,D\phi(\hat z))<0 .$$
Then for every sufficiently small $\kappa>0$ there is a viscosity subsolution
$W_\kappa$ of the same equation in $U$ with
$$W_\kappa\ge w\ \text{on }U,\qquad \sup_U(W_\kappa-w)>0,\qquad W_\kappa=w\ \text{on }\{z\in U:|z-\hat z|\ge\kappa\}.$$
Moreover $W_\kappa$ can be taken to be $\max(w,\chi)$ on a small ball around
$\hat z$ and $w$ outside it, where $\chi$ is a classical subsolution with
$\chi(\hat z)=w_*(\hat z)+\delta$ for some $\delta>0$. No choice principle is
used.
items.strategy: Strictify the lower contact without changing its first jet: for small γ>0 put φ̃(z)=φ(z)−γ|z−ẑ|⁴. Since the contact is a local minimum of w_*−φ, on a sufficiently small closed ball B̄(ẑ,r) one has w_*(z)−φ̃(z)≥m+γ|z−ẑ|⁴, where m=w_*(ẑ)−φ(ẑ). By continuity of H and the unchanged first jet, shrink r so φ̃_t+H(z,Dφ̃)≤−c/2 throughout the ball; thus every vertical translate of φ̃ is a classical subsolution there. Choose 0<δ<γ(r/2)⁴ and define χ=φ̃+m+δ. At ẑ, χ(ẑ)=w_*(ẑ)+δ. On the annulus r/2≤|z−ẑ|≤r, the strict quartic gap gives w_*(z)−χ(z)≥γ|z−ẑ|⁴−δ>0, so χ<w there. By the definition of the lower envelope, points z_j→ẑ exist with w(z_j)→w_*(ẑ); for large j, χ(z_j)>w(z_j). Hence W=max(w,χ) in the ball and W=w outside is a well-defined strict raise that agrees with w near the outer boundary. It is a subsolution because χ and w are subsolutions and finite maxima preserve subsolutions ([[prop-maxima-of-subsolutions-and-minima-of-supersolutions]]). Choosing the ball inside the requested support proves the claim. The annulus separation comes from strict quartic contact; a non-strict quadratic lower bound alone would not separate χ from w. P: a strict test-function bump plus the finite-maximum rule. S: [CIL] Lemma 4.4 and its proof, printed pp. 24–25; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 8, the supersolution half of the Perron proof, printed pp. 34–37.

items.title: Time-space barriers enforce the initial trace for the Cauchy problem
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open, $Z=O\times(0,T)$, let
$H:O\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let
$u_0\in C^1(O)$ have bounded gradient. Assume
$C_0:=\sup_{x\in O,\,0\le t\le T}|H(x,t,Du_0(x))|<\infty$. Define
$\phi_\pm(x,t):=u_0(x)\pm C_0t$. Then: (1) $\phi_-$ is a classical
subsolution and $\phi_+$ a classical supersolution in $Z$, each with initial
datum $u_0$; (2) if $w:Z\to\mathbb R$ is locally bounded with
$\phi_-\le w\le\phi_+$ on $Z$, then for every $x\in O$ the relaxed limits
satisfy
$$\liminf_{\substack{(y,s)\to(x,0)\\ s>0}}w(y,s)\ge u_0(x)\ge\limsup_{\substack{(y,s)\to(x,0)\\ s>0}}w(y,s),$$
so both equal $u_0(x)$; (3) consequently $w$ satisfies the relaxed initial
condition for the Cauchy problem in both directions, and any continuous
extension of $w$ to the initial face takes the value $u_0$ pointwise. No
choice principle is used.
items.strategy: For (1), at every (x,t)∈Z the time derivative of φ− is −C₀ and that of φ+ is C₀, while |H(x,t,Du₀(x))|≤C₀ by the stated supremum over both x and t. Hence (φ−)_t+H(x,t,Dφ−)≤0 and (φ+)_t+H(x,t,Dφ+)≥0. For (2), φ−(y,s)=u₀(y)−C₀s≤w(y,s)≤u₀(y)+C₀s=φ+(y,s); as (y,s)→(x,0), continuity of u₀ gives both relaxed limits equal u₀(x). This is the boundary squeeze used by the Perron construction. P: explicit affine-in-time barriers and continuity of the datum. S: [TR] Chapter 1 Section 8, Theorem 1.30, printed pp. 36–37; [CIL] (8.4)(IC) and Theorem 8.2, printed pp. 49–51.

items.title: Perron's method for the Cauchy problem: existence between two barriers
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, let
$H:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ satisfy the Lipschitz
conditions of part (a) of
[[thm-comparison-for-first-order-hamilton-jacobi-equations]], and let
$u_0\in C^1(\mathbb R^n)$ be bounded with bounded gradient. Assume
$C_0:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n,\,0\le t\le T}|H(x,t,Du_0(x))|<\infty$, and put
$\phi_\pm=u_0\pm C_0t$ as in
[[lem-viscosity-initial-trace-is-enforced-by-upper-and-lower-barriers]]. Define
$W(x,t)$ on $Z=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$ as the supremum of all viscosity
subsolutions $w$ with $\phi_-\le w\le\phi_+$ on $Z$. Then: (1) $W$ is well
defined and $\phi_-\le W\le\phi_+$; (2) $W^*$ is a viscosity subsolution and
$W_*$ is a viscosity supersolution in $Z$; (3) comparison gives
$W^*\le W_*$, hence $W=W^*=W_*$ is continuous, solves the Cauchy problem and
carries datum $u_0$ in the relaxed sense; (4) $W$ is the unique viscosity
solution in the class lying between $\phi_-$ and $\phi_+$. No choice principle
is used.
items.strategy: Well-definedness: $\phi_-$ itself is an admissible subsolution ([[lem-viscosity-initial-trace-is-enforced-by-upper-and-lower-barriers]]), so the defining family is nonempty, and $W$ is squeezed between the barriers, hence locally bounded above; by [[thm-upper-semicontinuous-envelope-of-a-locally-bounded-supremum-of-subsolutions]] the envelope $W^*$ is a subsolution, and $W^*\le\phi_+$ because the envelope of a family bounded above by $\phi_+$ is bounded above by the (continuous) $\phi_+$; since $W^*\ge W$ is then itself an admissible member of the family, $W^*\le W$ and hence $W=W^*$ is upper semicontinuous. If $W_*$ failed the supersolution test at some $\hat z$, then [[lem-perron-envelope-failure-of-the-supersolution-test-allows-a-local-bump]] gives a subsolution $W_\kappa\ge W$ with strict excess at some point in its support; at a strict failure point one has $W_*(\hat z)<\phi_+(\hat z)$ (otherwise $\phi_+-\phi$ would have a local minimum at $\hat z$ and the supersolution test for $\phi_+$ would give the non-strict inequality), so choose a positive vertical offset $\delta$ with $\chi(\hat z)=W_*(\hat z)+\delta<\phi_+(\hat z)$ and shrink the bump ball until $\chi\le\phi_+$ there, which keeps $W_\kappa\le\phi_+$; it is supported in the interior of the cylinder, away from the initial face and the barriers, its initial trace is still squeezed by the barriers, and hence it is admissible, contradicting the maximality of $W$. Hence $W_*$ is a supersolution; comparison ([[thm-comparison-for-first-order-hamilton-jacobi-equations]]) applied to the bounded upper semicontinuous subsolution $W^*$ and the bounded lower semicontinuous supersolution $W_*$, whose initial data both equal $u_0$ by [[lem-viscosity-initial-trace-is-enforced-by-upper-and-lower-barriers]], gives $W^*\le W_*$; combined with $W_*\le W\le W^*$ this forces $W=W^*=W_*$, so $W$ is continuous and is a viscosity solution attaining the data. Uniqueness follows from [[cor-uniqueness-of-bounded-uniformly-continuous-viscosity-solutions]]: any other solution squeezed by the barriers belongs to the defining family and is $\le W$, while comparison with $W$ gives the reverse inequality. P: envelope subsolution + bump contradiction + comparison. S: [TR] Chapter 1 Section 8, Theorem 1.30 and Remark 1.31, printed pp. 36--38; [CIL] Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 4.4, printed pp. 22--25; [BHJ] Section 5, comparison and existence, printed pp. 14--20.

items.title: The Legendre transform of a finite-valued convex Hamiltonian
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be finite-valued. The
**Legendre transform** (convex conjugate) of $H$ is the function
$L:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]) defined by
$$L(v):=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\bigl(p\cdot v-H(p)\bigr),\qquad v\in\mathbb R^n,$$
the supremum being taken in $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[lem-extended-reals-complete]]) and the inner product being the Euclidean one
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). The value $L(v)=+\infty$ is possible and is
not excluded.

In the biconjugate expressions $p\cdot v-(+\infty)$ the convention
$$p\cdot v-(+\infty):=-\infty$$
is adopted, so that the supremum defining the biconjugate
$L^*(p):=\sup_{v\in\mathbb R^n}\bigl(p\cdot v-L(v)\bigr)$ is an ordinary
supremum of a set in $\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}$ when the value $+\infty$
occurs: every $v$ with $L(v)=+\infty$ contributes the value $-\infty$ and can
be discarded.

When $H$ is convex
([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]), $L$ is the
convex conjugate used in the Hopf--Lax construction. For every finite-valued
$H$ the transform $L$ is convex and lower semicontinuous, being the pointwise
supremum of the affine functions $v\mapsto p\cdot v-H(p)$; no superlinearity,
differentiability, strict convexity, coercivity or smoothness of $H$ is
assumed at this point. The notation $H^*$ is used interchangeably with $L$.
items.strategy: Definition and notational contract; no proof. The transform is defined for every finite-valued $H$, convex or not, as the pointwise supremum of the affine functions $v\mapsto p\cdot v-H(p)$; convexity and lower semicontinuity of $L$ are immediate in that generality and are recorded so that they are not reproved later. The convention $p\cdot v-(+\infty)=-\infty$ fixes the meaning of the biconjugate $L^*(p)=\sup_v(p\cdot v-L(v))$ when $L$ is not finite everywhere, and it is the convention under which the supremum defining $L^*$ is nonempty and monotone in the natural way. The transform is stated for Hamiltonians on all of $\mathbb R^n$ and for finite-valued $H$, which is the exact class in which the biconjugacy lemma [[lem-finite-valued-convex-hamiltonian-equals-its-biconjugate]] is proved; the later Hopf--Lax regime adds superlinearity to make $L$ finite everywhere, a separate hypothesis. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Section 4, Definition 2.11 and Remark 2.12, printed p. 61; [TR] Appendix, the characterization of the Legendre transform, printed pp. 246--247; [CIL] the convex-duality discussion of Section 1, printed pp. 6--8.

items.title: A finite-valued convex Hamiltonian equals its biconjugate
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be convex
([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]), with Legendre
transform $L$ as in [[def-legendre-transform-of-a-hamiltonian]] and the
convention $p\cdot v-(+\infty):=-\infty$. Then for every $p\in\mathbb R^n$
$$H(p)=\sup_{v\in\mathbb R^n}\bigl(p\cdot v-L(v)\bigr),$$
so that $H=L^*=H^{**}$ is the biconjugate of $H$. Equivalently, the Moreau envelopes
$$e_\lambda H(p):=\inf_{q\in\mathbb R^n}\Bigl\{H(q)+\frac{|p-q|^2}{2\lambda}\Bigr\}\qquad(\lambda>0)$$
satisfy $e_\lambda H\le L^*\le H$ for every $\lambda>0$, and
$e_\lambda H(p)\to H(p)$ as $\lambda\downarrow0$ for every $p$. No
superlinearity, differentiability, smoothness, coercivity or strict convexity
of $H$ is assumed, and no choice principle is used; in particular the
supporting-hyperplane route is not needed.
items.strategy: The inequality $L^*(p)\le H(p)$ is elementary: by the definition of $L$, every $v$ satisfies $L(v)\ge p\cdot v-H(p)$, that is $p\cdot v-L(v)\le H(p)$, and taking the supremum over $v$ gives $L^*(p)\le H(p)$ (the convention $p\cdot v-(+\infty)=-\infty$ makes the same inequality vacuous when $L(v)=+\infty$). For the reverse inequality fix $p$ and $\lambda>0$ and put $\varphi(q):=H(q)+|p-q|^2/(2\lambda)$, so that $e_\lambda H(p)=\inf_q\varphi(q)$. The finite convex function $H$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^n$ ([[cor-convex-functions-on-open-convex-sets-are-continuous]]) and admits a lower affine bound: the continuous function $H$ has a finite minimum $m$ on the unit sphere ([[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]), and convexity along the ray $q=|q|u$ with $|u|=1$ gives $H(q)\ge|q|H(u)-(|q|-1)H(0)\ge-(|m|+|H(0)|)|q|$ for $|q|\ge1$. Hence $\varphi$ is continuous and coercive, and a nonempty sublevel set of $\varphi$ is closed and bounded, hence compact, so $\varphi$ attains its infimum at some $q_*\in\mathbb R^n$. At a minimiser, minimality applied at $q_*+r(q-q_*)$ with $r\in(0,1]$, together with the convexity inequality $H(q_*+r(q-q_*))\le(1-r)H(q_*)+rH(q)$, gives $H(q)\ge H(q_*)+v_*\cdot(q-q_*)$ for every $q\in\mathbb R^n$, where $v_*:=(p-q_*)/\lambda$: divide the two-point inequality by $r>0$ and let $r\downarrow0$. Consequently $L(v_*)=\sup_q(q\cdot v_*-H(q))=q_*\cdot v_*-H(q_*)$, so $$L^*(p)\ge p\cdot v_*-L(v_*)=(p-q_*)\cdot v_*+H(q_*)=\frac{|p-q_*|^2}{\lambda}+H(q_*)\ge H(q_*)+\frac{|p-q_*|^2}{2\lambda}=e_\lambda H(p).$$ Finally $e_\lambda H(p)\to H(p)$ as $\lambda\downarrow0$: the competitor $q=p$ gives $e_\lambda H(p)\le H(p)$; for the lower bound fix $\varepsilon>0$ and $\delta>0$ with $|H(q)-H(p)|\le\varepsilon$ for $|q-p|\le\delta$ (continuity at $p$); for $r=|q-p|\le\delta$ one has $\varphi(q)\ge H(p)-\varepsilon+r^2/(2\lambda)$, and for $r\ge\delta$ two-point convexity along the ray from $p$ through $q$ gives $H(q)\ge H(p)-(\varepsilon/\delta)r$, so $\varphi(q)\ge H(p)-(\varepsilon/\delta)r+r^2/(2\lambda)$; for $\lambda\le\delta^2/\varepsilon$ the minimum of the latter expression over $r\ge\delta$ is at least $H(p)-\varepsilon$, so $e_\lambda H(p)\ge H(p)-\varepsilon$ for all small $\lambda$; letting $\lambda\downarrow0$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives $H(p)\le L^*(p)\le H(p)$, hence equality. The supporting inequality is derived at the attained Moreau minimiser from convexity and compactness instead of being imported from the published subgradient theorem, which states the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, so no choice principle is consumed; superlinearity, differentiability, smoothness, coercivity and strict convexity of $H$ are not used. P: conjugate monotonicity plus the attained Moreau minimiser. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Theorem 2.13(ii) and Remark 2.14, printed pp. 62--63; [TR] Appendix, the characterization of the Legendre transform, printed pp. 246--247; [CIL] the convex-duality discussion of Section 1, printed pp. 6--8.

items.title: The Hopf--Lax operator and the Hopf--Lax formula
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be convex and superlinear,
$$\lim_{|p|\to\infty}\frac{H(p)}{|p|}=+\infty,$$
let $L$ be its Legendre transform
([[def-legendre-transform-of-a-hamiltonian]]), and let
$u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]], [[def-bounded-set]]). For $t>0$ and
$x\in\mathbb R^n$ define
$$Q_tu_0(x):=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\Bigl\{u_0(y)+tL\Bigl(\frac{x-y}{t}\Bigr)\Bigr\},$$
the infimum being computed in $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[def-infimum]]) over the extended-real values
$u_0(y)+tL((x-y)/t)$; the term $tL((x-y)/t)$ is $+\infty$ exactly when
$L((x-y)/t)=+\infty$. Set $Q_0u_0:=u_0$.

The **Hopf--Lax operator** with Lagrangian $L$ is the family $(Q_t)_{t\ge0}$,
and the function $(x,t)\mapsto Q_tu_0(x)$ is the **Hopf--Lax formula** for the
Cauchy problem $u_t+H(Du)=0$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$. The infimum is an
extended-real expression at this point: finiteness and the confinement of
near-minimisers are proved in [[lem-hopf-lax-infima-localise]], where
superlinearity makes $L$ real-valued everywhere.
items.strategy: Definition and notational contract; no proof. The definition fixes (i) the autonomous Hamiltonian $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ convex and superlinear, (ii) the datum class: bounded and uniformly continuous $u_0$, (iii) the infimum over all $y\in\mathbb R^n$ of $u_0(y)+tL((x-y)/t)$ for $t>0$, read in the extended reals, and (iv) the value $Q_0u_0=u_0$. The design keeps the value $+\infty$ visible until finiteness is proved, so no assertion of attainability or of localisation is smuggled into the definition; $L$ is written with the convention of [[def-legendre-transform-of-a-hamiltonian]] and will be seen to be real-valued under superlinearity in [[lem-hopf-lax-infima-localise]]. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Sections 5.2--5.4, Definition 2.19 and equation (2.19), printed pp. 64--68; [BHJ] Section 2 and the discussion of the Hopf--Lax formula, printed pp. 6--9; [CIL] Section 1, the Hopf--Lax representation of the source, printed pp. 6--8.

items.title: Finiteness, superlinearity of the Lagrangian and localisation of Hopf--Lax near-minimisers
items.statement:
Let $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be convex and superlinear with Legendre
transform $L$, and let $u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and continuous.
Then: (1) $L$ is real-valued on $\mathbb R^n$, convex, continuous, and
superlinear; (2) for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and $t>0$ the infimum defining
$Q_tu_0(x)$ is attained, and for every $\delta>0$ there is a finite radius
$\rho=\rho(x,t,\delta,\|u_0\|_\infty)$ such that every near-minimiser $y$ with
$$u_0(y)+tL\Bigl(\frac{x-y}{t}\Bigr)\le Q_tu_0(x)+\delta$$
satisfies $|y-x|\le\rho$; (3) consequently $Q_tu_0$ is real-valued for every
$x$ and every $t\ge0$. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: For fixed v, superlinearity of H makes p·v−H(p) tend to −∞ as |p|→∞, so the supremum defining L(v) is finite and attained on a bounded set. Convexity of L is immediate. To prove superlinearity of L, fix any a>0. For v≠0, choose p=a v/|v|; then L(v)≥a|v|−max_{|q|≤a}H(q). The maximum is finite by continuity on the compact ball. Holding a fixed and dividing by |v| gives liminf_{|v|→∞}L(v)/|v|≥a; since a is arbitrary, L(v)/|v|→∞. Continuity of the finite convex L follows from [[cor-convex-functions-on-open-convex-sets-are-continuous]]. For localisation, use the competitor y=x, so Q_tu₀(x)≤||u₀||∞+tL(0). A δ-near-minimiser therefore has tL((x−y)/t)≤2||u₀||∞+δ+tL(0); superlinearity bounds |x−y|/t, yielding the radius ρ. The objective is continuous because u₀ and L are continuous, and every near-minimiser lies in the resulting compact ball, so the infimum is attained there by the extreme-value theorem. The same estimates give finiteness. P: coercivity of L confines near-minimisers, and continuity gives attainment. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Theorem 2.13(i) and Example 2.4, printed pp. 61–62 and 68; [TR] Exercise 26 on bounded level sets, printed p. 67; [BHJ] Section 2, localisation of the infimum, printed pp. 6–9.

items.title: The Hopf--Lax operator is a contraction in the supremum norm
items.statement:
Let $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be convex and superlinear with Legendre transform
$L$, and let $u_0,v_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Then for every $t\ge0$
and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$
$$\bigl|Q_tu_0(x)-Q_tv_0(x)\bigr|\le\sup_{\mathbb R^n}|u_0-v_0|,$$
and consequently $\sup_{\mathbb R^n}|Q_tu_0-Q_tv_0|\le\|u_0-v_0\|_\infty$; both
$Q_tu_0$ and $Q_tv_0$ are real-valued (see the proof for the explicit
finiteness argument). No uniform continuity of the data is needed for this
particular estimate, and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy: For t=0 the statement is the identity. For t>0, the conjugate L is bounded below because L(v)≥−H(0), while the competitor y=x gives a finite upper bound; hence both infima are real. For every y, u₀(y)+tL((x−y)/t)≤v₀(y)+tL((x−y)/t)+||u₀−v₀||∞. Taking infima gives Q_tu₀(x)−Q_tv₀(x)≤||u₀−v₀||∞; exchanging u₀ and v₀ gives the reverse bound. This argument uses only boundedness of the data and does not require minimisers or uniform continuity. P: compare the two infima with the same competitor. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Section 5.4, the contraction estimate for the Hopf–Lax formula, printed pp. 67–68; [BHJ] Section 2, continuous dependence of the formula on the datum, printed pp. 6–9.

items.title: The Hopf--Lax operator preserves a modulus of continuity
items.statement:
Let $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be convex and superlinear with Legendre
transform $L$, and let $u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and uniformly
continuous with a nondecreasing modulus of continuity $\omega$ satisfying
$\omega(r)\to0$ as $r\downarrow0$ and
$|u_0(y)-u_0(y')|\le\omega(|y-y'|)$. Then for every $t\ge0$ and all
$x,x'\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$|Q_tu_0(x)-Q_tu_0(x')|\le\omega(|x-x'|).$$
Thus every $Q_tu_0$ has the same modulus of continuity and the family is
spatially equicontinuous; this is the equicontinuity input of the
initial-trace and vanishing-viscosity arguments. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Fix $x,x'\in\mathbb R^n$ and $d:=x-x'$. For $t>0$ and any $y'\in\mathbb R^n$ put $y:=y'+d$; then $(x-y)/t=(x'-y')/t$ and $u_0(y)\ge u_0(y')-\omega(|d|)$, so $u_0(y)+tL((x-y)/t)\ge u_0(y')+tL((x'-y')/t)-\omega(|d|)$. Taking the infimum over $y'$ (finite by [[lem-hopf-lax-infima-localise]]) gives $Q_tu_0(x)\ge Q_tu_0(x')-\omega(|d|)$; the reverse inequality follows by symmetry, and $t=0$ is the hypothesis itself. The estimate is translation invariant because the Hamiltonian is autonomous and $L$ does not depend on $y$: this is the structural reason the formula transfers the modulus of the datum to the solution. P: translate a competitor in the infimum. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Section 5.4, the modulus-of-continuity estimate for (2.19), printed pp. 67--68; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 9, the role of a modulus of continuity in Perron and Lipschitz estimates, printed pp. 38--40; [BHJ] Section 2, the translation identity for the formula, printed pp. 6--9.

items.title: The Hopf--Lax operators form a semigroup (dynamic programming)
items.statement:
Let $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be convex and superlinear with Legendre
transform $L$, and let $u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and uniformly
continuous. Then for all $t,s\ge0$ the Hopf--Lax operators of
[[def-hopf-lax-operator]] satisfy
$$Q_{t+s}u_0=Q_t(Q_su_0)=Q_s(Q_tu_0)\qquad\text{pointwise on }\mathbb R^n,$$
where the inner operators are applied to the bounded uniformly continuous
function $Q_su_0$ (or $Q_tu_0$) produced by
[[cor-hopf-lax-preserves-a-modulus-of-continuity]]. Equivalently, for all
$t,s>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R^n$ the short-time variational principle holds:
$$Q_{t+s}u_0(x)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R^n}\Bigl\{Q_su_0(z)+tL\Bigl(\frac{x-z}{t}\Bigr)\Bigr\}.$$
The family $(Q_t)_{t\ge0}$ is therefore a semigroup with $Q_0=\mathrm{id}$ on
the bounded uniformly continuous data. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Both inequalities are the two-point convexity inequality of $L$ with weights adapted to $t$ and $s$. For the inequality $Q_{t+s}u_0(x)\le Q_t(Q_su_0)(x)$: given $y,z\in\mathbb R^n$, write $x-y=(x-z)+(z-y)$ and $L\bigl(\frac{x-y}{t+s}\bigr)=L\bigl(\frac{t}{t+s}\frac{x-z}{t}+\frac{s}{t+s}\frac{z-y}{s}\bigr)\le\frac{t}{t+s}L\bigl(\frac{x-z}{t}\bigr)+\frac{s}{t+s}L\bigl(\frac{z-y}{s}\bigr)$ by convexity of $L$; multiplying by $t+s$ and adding $u_0(y)$ gives $u_0(y)+(t+s)L((x-y)/(t+s))\le u_0(y)+sL((z-y)/s)+tL((x-z)/t)$, and taking the infimum over $y$ and then $z$ gives the claim (the double infimum is the infimum over pairs, which is legitimate for extended-real infima). For the reverse inequality: given $y$, choose the point $z:=y+\frac{s}{t+s}(x-y)$, for which $\frac{z-y}{s}=\frac{x-z}{t}=\frac{x-y}{t+s}$; then $u_0(y)+sL((z-y)/s)+tL((x-z)/t)=u_0(y)+(t+s)L((x-y)/(t+s))$, so $Q_t(Q_su_0)(x)\le u_0(y)+(t+s)L((x-y)/(t+s))$, and taking the infimum over $y$ gives $Q_tQ_su_0\le Q_{t+s}u_0$. The reverse order is identical, which also yields the variational principle. The composition is legitimate because [[cor-hopf-lax-preserves-a-modulus-of-continuity]] keeps $Q_su_0$ bounded and uniformly continuous, so the inner operator is defined. P: two-point convexity plus the infimum over the plane point on the segment. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Theorem 2.21 (dynamic programming principle) and its proof, printed pp. 65--67; [BHJ] Section 2, the semigroup property of the Lagrangian formula, printed pp. 6--9; [CIL] Section 1, dynamic programming for first-order equations, printed pp. 6--8.

items.title: A Hopf--Lax minimiser satisfies the characteristic Euler relation at differentiability points
items.statement:
Let $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be convex and superlinear with Legendre
transform $L$, let $u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and continuous, and
let $t>0$, $x\in\mathbb R^n$. Let $y$ be a minimiser of
$\varphi(y):=u_0(y)+tL((x-y)/t)$, which exists by
[[lem-hopf-lax-infima-localise]], put $v:=(x-y)/t$, and set $u:=Q_tu_0$. Then:
(1) if $u_0$ is differentiable at $y$ and $L$ is differentiable at $v$, then
$Du_0(y)=DL(v)$; (2) if $L$ is differentiable at $v$ and $u$ is
differentiable at $x$, then $Du(x)=DL(v)$. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Minimality of $y$ gives, for every $h\in\mathbb R^n$ small, $u_0(y)+tL(v)\le u_0(y+h)+tL(v-h/t)$; expanding both sides by differentiability at the respective points gives $u_0(y)+tL(v)\le u_0(y)+\langle Du_0(y),h\rangle+tL(v)-\langle DL(v),h\rangle+o(|h|)$, hence $0\le\langle Du_0(y)-DL(v),h\rangle+o(|h|)$ for all small $h$; applying the inequality with $h$ and with $-h$ and dividing by $|h|$ gives $Du_0(y)=DL(v)$, which is (1). For (2), minimality at $x$ gives for every $h$ small $Q_tu_0(x+h)\le u_0(y)+tL\bigl(v+h/t\bigr)=Q_tu_0(x)+\langle DL(v),h\rangle+o(|h|)$; since $Q_tu_0$ is differentiable at $x$, its increment is $Q_tu_0(x)+\langle Du(x),h\rangle+o(|h|)$, so $\langle Du(x)-DL(v),h\rangle\le o(|h|)$ for all small $h$ and, dividing by $|h|$ in both directions, $Du(x)=DL(v)$. The two conclusions are the first-order optimality conditions connecting the variational and characteristic pictures; differentiability is assumed only at the points where it is used, and no global smoothness of $u_0$, $L$ or $u$ is asserted. P: expand the minimality inequality to first order in the direction of the perturbation. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Section 5.4, the characteristic relation for (2.19), printed pp. 67--68; [BHJ] Section 1, characteristics and the envelope relation, printed pp. 2--6.

items.title: Comparison for autonomous convex superlinear Hamiltonians
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be finite-valued, continuous,
convex and superlinear. Let $T>0$. Suppose $u$ and $v$ are bounded uniformly
continuous on $\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]$, their restrictions to
$Z=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$ are respectively a viscosity subsolution and a
viscosity supersolution of $u_t+H(Du)=0$, and their continuous initial traces
satisfy $u(x,0)\le v(x,0)$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$. Then $u\le v$ on $Z$.
No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
Assume for contradiction that u(x₀,t₀)>v(x₀,t₀) at some 0<t₀<T. Choose δ,η,η′>0 so that U(x₀,t₀)−V(x₀,t₀)>3δ, where U(x,t)=u(x,t)−η/(T−t) and V(x,t)=v(x,t)+η′/(T−t); write B=η+η′. At every interior C¹ upper test φ for U, φ+η/(T−t) is an upper test for u, so φ_t+H(Dφ)≤−η/(T−t)²≤−η/T². At every lower test φ for V, φ−η′/(T−t) is a lower test for v, so φ_t+H(Dφ)≥η′/(T−t)²≥η′/T². Also U→−∞ and V→+∞ uniformly in x at t↑T.
Let ω₀ be a bounded modulus of continuity for v(·,0). Choose P>0 with sup_{r≥0}(ω₀(r)−Pr)<B/(8T), then choose ε>0 with Pε<B/(8T), and set ψ(r)=P(√(r²+ε²)−ε). Thus ψ(r)≥Pr−Pε and the smooth radial function z↦ψ(|z|) has gradient norm at most P. Let χ(x)=√(1+|x|²). Choose ρ>0 small enough that ρ≤1, Φα(x₀,x₀,t₀,t₀)>2δ for every α, and the modulus of continuity of H on |p|≤P+1 at radius 2ρ is less than B/T². For α>0 maximize
Φα(x,y,t,s)=U(x,t)−V(y,s)−ψ(|x−y|)−(α/2)|t−s|²−ρ(χ(x)+χ(y))
on x,y∈ℝⁿ and 0≤t,s≤T, defining Φα=−∞ on t=T or s=T. The bound on u,v, the coercive spatial term, and the terminal blow-down/up make each positive superlevel set compact; the Euclidean extreme-value theorem therefore gives a maximum. Its value is greater than 2δ by the choice of ρ. Since U−V is bounded above, α|t−s|² is bounded at maximizers; hence |t−s|→0 as α→∞. If t=0 at a sequence of maximizers, then s→0 and, using u₀≤v₀, ψ(r)≥Pr−Pε, and a time modulus ωᵥ for v, we have Φα≤sup_{r≥0}(ω₀(r)−Pr)+Pε−B/T+ωᵥ(s)<−3B/(4T)+ωᵥ(s), which is negative for large α; the case s=0 is identical using a time modulus for u. This contradicts the positive maximum, so for all sufficiently large α a maximizing point has 0<t,s<T.
At such a maximum, the C¹ contact gradients and time derivatives are
p=P(x−y)/√(|x−y|²+ε²)+ρDχ(x),  q=P(x−y)/√(|x−y|²+ε²)−ρDχ(y),  a=α(t−s).
Thus |p|,|q|≤P+1 and |p−q|≤2ρ. The strict viscosity inequalities give a+H(p)≤−η/T² and a+H(q)≥η′/T², hence B/T²≤H(q)−H(p). The choice of ρ makes |H(q)−H(p)|<B/T² whenever |p−q|≤2ρ. This contradiction proves u≤v on Z. The argument needs no global momentum-Lipschitz estimate; the stated finite continuous convex superlinear class includes H(p)=|p|²/2. P: bounded-gradient spatial doubling, a vanishing coercive weight, and strict terminal-time penalties, with initial faces controlled by the modulus of the ordered traces. S: [CIL] Theorem 8.3, printed pp. 51–52; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 6 and Chapter 2 around equation (2.18), printed pp. 26–29 and 66–68; [BHJ] Section 5, comparison, printed pp. 14–20.

items.title: The Hopf--Lax formula solves the Hamilton--Jacobi Cauchy problem
items.statement:
Let $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be finite-valued, continuous, convex, and
superlinear, with Legendre transform $L$, and let
$u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and uniformly continuous. Define
$u(x,t):=Q_tu_0(x)$ by [[def-hopf-lax-operator]]. Then $u$ is a bounded
uniformly continuous function on $\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]$ for every $T>0$, and:
(1) $u$ is a viscosity solution of $u_t+H(Du)=0$ in
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$; (2) $u$ attains the initial datum locally
uniformly,
$$\sup_{x\in K}|u(x,t)-u_0(x)|\longrightarrow0\qquad(t\downarrow0)$$
for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$; (3) $u$ is the unique bounded
uniformly continuous viscosity solution of the Cauchy problem with datum
$u_0$; (4) $u$ satisfies the dynamic-programming relation
$Q_{t+s}u_0=Q_tQ_su_0$ of
[[thm-hopf-lax-dynamic-programming-semigroup]]. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Boundedness and uniform continuity: $u$ is bounded by $\|u_0\|_\infty+t\max\{L(0),0\}$ together with the lower bound $\inf L$ (finite by superlinearity) on compact time intervals, and it is uniformly continuous in $x$ with the modulus of $u_0$ by [[cor-hopf-lax-preserves-a-modulus-of-continuity]] and in $t$ because $|Q_tu_0(x)-Q_su_0(x)|\le\|Q_{|t-s|}u_0-u_0\|_\infty$ for $t,s\ge0$, which follows from the semigroup law [[thm-hopf-lax-dynamic-programming-semigroup]] and the contraction [[cor-hopf-lax-is-a-contraction-in-the-supremum-norm]], while $\|Q_\tau u_0-u_0\|_\infty\to0$ as $\tau\downarrow0$ because $Q_\tau u_0(x)\le u_0(x)+\tau L(0)$ and $Q_\tau u_0(x)\ge\inf_v\{u_0(x-\tau v)+\tau L(v)\}\ge u_0(x)-\sup_v\{\omega(\tau|v|)-\tau L(v)\}$ with the modulus $\omega$ of $u_0$ and the superlinearity of $L$. Subsolution: let $\phi\in C^1$, let $u-\phi$ have a strict local maximum at $(x_0,t_0)$ with $t_0>0$. For small $h>0$ and each $v\in\mathbb R^n$ put $y:=x_0-hv$; the dynamic-programming inequality $u(x_0,t_0)\le u(y,t_0-h)+hL(v)$ (from the variational principle of [[thm-hopf-lax-dynamic-programming-semigroup]]) and the contact inequality $u(y,t_0-h)\le u(x_0,t_0)-\phi(x_0,t_0)+\phi(y,t_0-h)$ combine to $\phi(x_0,t_0)-\phi(x_0-hv,t_0-h)\le hL(v)+o(h)$; dividing by $h$ and letting $h\downarrow0$ gives $\phi_t(x_0,t_0)+\langle D\phi(x_0,t_0),v\rangle\le L(v)$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$, and taking the supremum over $v$ and using the biconjugacy $H=L^*$ of [[lem-finite-valued-convex-hamiltonian-equals-its-biconjugate]] gives $\phi_t+H(D\phi(x_0,t_0))\le0$. Supersolution: let $u-\phi$ have a strict local minimum at $(x_0,t_0)$, $t_0>0$; let $y$ be a minimiser for $u(x_0,t_0)$ at time $t_0$ ([[lem-hopf-lax-infima-localise]]) and put $v:=(x_0-y)/t_0$. For $0<h<t_0$ put $z_h:=y+\frac{t_0-h}{t_0}(x_0-y)$, so that $z_h\to x_0$ and $(z_h-y)/(t_0-h)=(x_0-y)/t_0=v$. Evaluating the variational principle of [[thm-hopf-lax-dynamic-programming-semigroup]] at $(z_h,t_0-h)$ with the single competitor $y$ gives $u(z_h,t_0-h)+hL(v)\le u_0(y)+(t_0-h)L(v)+hL(v)=u_0(y)+t_0L(v)=u(x_0,t_0)$, hence $u(x_0,t_0)-u(z_h,t_0-h)\ge hL(v)$; the local-minimum contact at $(x_0,t_0)$ applies to the nearby point $(z_h,t_0-h)$ and gives $u(z_h,t_0-h)\ge u(x_0,t_0)-\phi(x_0,t_0)+\phi(z_h,t_0-h)$. Combining, $\phi(x_0,t_0)-\phi(z_h,t_0-h)\ge hL(v)$; dividing by $h$ and letting $h\downarrow0$ along $z_h$ gives $\phi_t(x_0,t_0)+\langle D\phi(x_0,t_0),v\rangle\ge L(v)$, and the elementary inequality $H(p)=\sup_w(p\cdot w-L(w))\ge p\cdot v-L(v)$ gives the supersolution inequality. Initial trace: the bounds $u_0(x)-\sup_v\{\omega(\tau|v|)-\tau L(v)\}\le Q_\tau u_0(x)\le u_0(x)+\tau L(0)$ hold uniformly in $x$, and $\sup_v\{\omega(\tau|v|)-\tau L(v)\}\to0$ as $\tau\downarrow0$ by superlinearity of $L$; the local-uniform statement follows. Uniqueness in the stated class follows from [[thm-comparison-for-autonomous-convex-superlinear-hamiltonians]], since every finite-valued convex superlinear H in this theorem satisfies that comparison theorem’s hypotheses and the Hopf–Lax solution is bounded uniformly continuous on each closed finite-time slab. The global momentum-Lipschitz comparison case (a) is not used here; it would exclude H(p)=|p|²/2. P: the dynamic-programming inequality in both directions plus the biconjugacy.
