items.title: Vanishing viscosity selects the viscosity solution
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $Z=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$, and
$Z_0=\mathbb R^n\times[0,T)$. Let
$H:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ satisfy the
Lipschitz conditions of part (a) of
[[thm-comparison-for-first-order-hamilton-jacobi-equations]], let
$u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and uniformly continuous, and let
$u_0^{(\varepsilon)}\to u_0$ locally uniformly on $\mathbb R^n$. For each
$\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ let $u^\varepsilon:Z\to\mathbb R$ be a viscosity
solution of
$$u^\varepsilon_t+H(x,t,Du^\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\Delta u^\varepsilon\qquad\text{in }Z,$$
meaning that for every test function $\phi\in C^{1,2}(Z)$ the residual
$\phi_t+H(z,D\phi)-\varepsilon\Delta\phi$ is nonpositive at each local
maximum of $u^\varepsilon-\phi$ and nonnegative at each local minimum. Assume
that $u^\varepsilon$ has initial datum $u_0^{(\varepsilon)}$ in the relaxed
Cauchy sense. Suppose the family is uniformly bounded on $Z$ and locally
equicontinuous up to the initial face: there is $M<\infty$ with
$|u^\varepsilon(z)|\le M$ for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $z\in Z$, and
for every compact $K\subseteq Z_0$ and every $\eta>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such
that
$$|u^\varepsilon(z)-u^\varepsilon(z')|<\eta$$
for all $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $z,z'\in K\cap Z$ with $|z-z'|<\delta$.
These estimates give each $u^\varepsilon$ a continuous trace on the initial
face. Then $u^\varepsilon\to u$ locally uniformly on $Z$, where $u$ is the
unique bounded viscosity solution of $u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ with datum $u_0$. Neither
existence of the approximants nor a compactness theorem is asserted: the
boundedness and equicontinuity estimates are hypotheses. No choice principle is
used.
items.strategy: Let $\overline u$ and $\underline u$ be the upper and lower half-relaxed limits of the family ([[def-half-relaxed-limits]]). At a local maximum of $u^\varepsilon-\phi$, the viscosity inequality for the viscous equation reads $\phi_t(z,D\phi)+H(z,D\phi)\le\varepsilon\Delta\phi(z)$; since $\Delta\phi$ is bounded on the compact set carrying the contact points, the right side is a perturbation $c_\varepsilon\to0$ locally uniformly, and the perturbed stability theorem [[thm-half-relaxed-limit-stability-for-viscosity-solutions]] gives that $\overline u$ is a viscosity subsolution of the limit equation; the lower relaxed limit is a supersolution by the dual statement. The initial data pass to the limit because the local equicontinuity of the family up to the initial face turns the relaxed limsup of a sequence approaching $(x,0)$ into the limsup of the data $u_0^{(\varepsilon)}(y)$, which converges to $u_0(x)$. Comparison [[thm-comparison-for-first-order-hamilton-jacobi-equations]] applied to the bounded upper semicontinuous subsolution $\overline u$ and the bounded lower semicontinuous supersolution $\underline u$, whose initial data both equal $u_0$, gives $\overline u\le\underline u$; since $\underline u\le\overline u$ by definition, $\overline u=\underline u=:u$, which is therefore continuous and is the unique bounded viscosity solution ([[cor-uniqueness-of-bounded-uniformly-continuous-viscosity-solutions]]). The pointwise agreement of the two relaxed limits is equivalent to locally uniform convergence of the family: if not, there are a compact $K$, $\delta>0$ and sequences $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$, $z_j\in K$ with $|u^{\varepsilon_j}(z_j)-u(z_j)|\ge\delta$; passing to a convergent subsequence $z_j\to z_*\in K$ contradicts the equality of the limsup and liminf at $z_*$ and the continuity of $u$. Local boundedness of the family is what makes the relaxed limits well defined, and no sequence of indices is selected anywhere: this is the exact sense in which the theorem uses item 9 and avoids asserting compactness. P: half-relaxed limits, stability with a vanishing perturbation, comparison, and a compactness-free conversion to local uniform convergence. S: [TR] Chapter 1 Section 3, Theorem 1.9 and its proof, printed pp. 19--21, and Remark 1.10, printed p. 21; [CIL] Section 6, Theorem 6.1 and the half-relaxed limit method, printed pp. 38--42; [BHJ] Section 4, stability and the vanishing-viscosity limit, printed pp. 12--14.

items.title: Finite speed of dependence for Hamiltonians Lipschitz in momentum
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, and let
$H:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Suppose
there are constants $C>0$ and $L>0$ such that, for all $x,y,p,q\in\mathbb R^n$
and $t,s\in[0,T]$,
$$|H(x,t,p)-H(y,s,p)|\le C(1+|p|)(|x-y|+|t-s|),\qquad |H(x,t,p)-H(x,t,q)|\le L|p-q|.$$
Let $u,v:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R$ be bounded, with $u$ upper
semicontinuous and $v$ lower semicontinuous; assume that $u$ is a viscosity
subsolution and $v$ a viscosity supersolution of $u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$. Fix $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ and $R>0$. If
$u(x,0)\le v(x,0)$ for every $x\in B(x_0,R)$, then
$$u(x,t)\le v(x,t)\qquad\text{for }0\le t<\min\{T,R/L\}\text{ and }|x-x_0|<R-Lt.$$
In particular, if $u$ and $v$ are bounded viscosity solutions with the same
initial values on $B(x_0,R)$ and are also respectively lower and upper
semicontinuous on $\mathbb R^n\times[0,T)$ (so both are continuous there),
then $u(x,t)=v(x,t)$ on this open backward cone.
The cone is stated with strict spatial inequality because $B(x_0,R)$ is open
and no continuity of the initial traces is assumed. No choice principle is
used.
items.strategy:
Put $w:=u-v$, which is bounded and upper semicontinuous. First show that $w$ is a viscosity subsolution of $w_t-L|Dw|=0$. Let $\phi\in C^1$ touch $w$ from above at an interior point $(x_*,t_*)$. Choose $T_*$ with $t_*<T_*<T$ and restrict $u,v$ to the closed slab $\mathbb R^n\times[0,T_*]$. Add a positive quadratic vanishing to first order at this point, so the contact becomes strict, and choose a compact cylinder $Q\Subset\mathbb R^n\times(0,T_*)$ around it on whose boundary the strictified contact is lower. Apply the $[0,T_*]$ version of the localization lemma; for fixed $\rho>0$, maximize on $Q\times Q$ the upper semicontinuous function
$$F_{\alpha,\rho}(x,y,t,s):=u(x,t)-v(y,s)-\phi(x,t)-\frac\alpha2(|x-y|^2+|t-s|^2)-\rho(|x-x_*|^2+|y-x_*|^2).$$
Its diagonal limiting function is $w(x,t)-\phi(x,t)-2\rho|x-x_*|^2$, which has a strict maximum at $(x_*,t_*)$. Thus for large $\alpha$ the maximizing points $(x_\alpha,y_\alpha,t_\alpha,s_\alpha)$ remain interior to $Q$ (in particular below $T_*$) and converge to $(x_*,x_*,t_*,t_*)$. The localization calculation of [[lem-doubling-variables-maximum-localisation]] gives $\alpha d_\alpha^2\to0$, where $d_\alpha^2:=|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|^2+|t_\alpha-s_\alpha|^2$: if $M_\alpha:=\max F_{\alpha,\rho}$, then $M_\alpha\downarrow w(x_*,t_*)-\phi(x_*,t_*)$ and $M_{\alpha/2}\ge M_\alpha+\alpha d_\alpha^2/4$. The $C^1$ contacts for $u$ and $v$ have spatial gradients
$$p_\alpha=D\phi(x_\alpha,t_\alpha)+\alpha(x_\alpha-y_\alpha)+2\rho(x_\alpha-x_*),\qquad q_\alpha=\alpha(x_\alpha-y_\alpha)-2\rho(y_\alpha-x_*),$$
and both time derivatives contain the same term $\alpha(t_\alpha-s_\alpha)$, the time derivative for $u$ having the additional $\phi_t(x_\alpha,t_\alpha)$. The viscosity inequalities therefore give
$$\phi_t(x_\alpha,t_\alpha)\le H(y_\alpha,s_\alpha,q_\alpha)-H(x_\alpha,t_\alpha,p_\alpha)\le L|q_\alpha-p_\alpha|+C(1+|p_\alpha|)(|x_\alpha-y_\alpha|+|t_\alpha-s_\alpha|).$$
The last term tends to zero because $\alpha d_\alpha^2\to0$ and $D\phi$ is bounded near the contact. Also $q_\alpha-p_\alpha=-D\phi(x_\alpha,t_\alpha)-2\rho((x_\alpha-x_*)+(y_\alpha-x_*))\to-D\phi(x_*,t_*)$. Hence $\phi_t(x_*,t_*)-L|D\phi(x_*,t_*)|\le0$. In particular the difference of spatial test gradients is not discarded: it converges to the test gradient $D\phi$ and produces the term $L|D\phi|$.

Now let $M:=\max\{0,\sup_{\mathbb R^n\times[0,T)}w\}$. Fix $0<\epsilon<R$ and use the explicit nondecreasing $C^1$ cutoff $h(s)=0$ for $s\le0$, $h(s)=3s^2-2s^3$ for $0\le s\le1$, and $h(s)=1$ for $s\ge1$. Set $\xi_\epsilon(r):=M h((r-(R-\epsilon))/\epsilon)$. For $\delta>0$ define the smooth radial barrier
$$\psi_{\epsilon,\delta}(x,t):=\xi_\epsilon\bigl(\sqrt{|x-x_0|^2+\delta^2}+Lt\bigr).$$
It is a supersolution of $\psi_t-L|D\psi|=0$, since $\xi_\epsilon'\ge0$ and
$$\partial_t\psi_{\epsilon,\delta}-L|D\psi_{\epsilon,\delta}|=L\xi_\epsilon'\left(1-\frac{|x-x_0|}{\sqrt{|x-x_0|^2+\delta^2}}\right)\ge0.$$
At $t=0$, if $|x-x_0|<R$, then $w(x,0)\le0\le\psi_{\epsilon,\delta}(x,0)$; if $|x-x_0|\ge R$, the cutoff equals $M$, so again $w(x,0)\le\psi_{\epsilon,\delta}(x,0)$. Apply the whole-space comparison theorem [[thm-comparison-for-first-order-hamilton-jacobi-equations]] to $w$ and $\psi_{\epsilon,\delta}$ for the Hamiltonian $G(p)=-L|p|$. For any point with $|x-x_0|+Lt<R$, choose $\epsilon>0$ and then $\delta>0$ sufficiently small that $\sqrt{|x-x_0|^2+\delta^2}+Lt\le R-\epsilon$. At that point $\psi_{\epsilon,\delta}=0$, hence $w\le0$. Applying the result in both orders gives equality for two solutions with equal initial data on the ball. The cutoff is explicit and the proof uses no choice principle. P: reduce the difference by a localized two-time doubling argument, then compare with a smooth radial cone barrier. S: [TR] Chapter 1 Section 10, Lemma 1.36, Lemma 1.37 and Theorem 1.35, printed pp. 40--42; [BHJ] Section 5, comparison and domains of dependence, printed pp. 14--20; [CIL] Section 5.B, finite speed as a consequence of comparison, printed pp. 34--36.

items.title: Value functions and the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation: orientation only
items.statement:
For a controlled dynamical system $y'(\cdot)=b(y,v)$ with running cost
$L(y,v)$ and initial cost $u_0$, consider the **value function**
$$u(x,t)=\inf\Bigl\{\int_0^tL\bigl(\gamma(s),v(s)\bigr)\,ds+u_0\bigl(\gamma(0)\bigr):\ \gamma(t)=x,\ \gamma'=b(\gamma,v)\Bigr\}$$
over admissible controls. When hypotheses make this value finite and
continuous, ensure the dynamic programming principle, and give the viscosity
characterization, $u$ is a viscosity solution of the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman
equation $u_t+H(x,Du)=0$ with
$$H(x,p)=\sup_v\{p\cdot b(x,v)-L(x,v)\}.$$
To express the Legendre duality precisely, define the effective velocity cost
$$\ell(x,\xi):=\inf\{L(x,v):b(x,v)=\xi\},$$
with value $+\infty$ when the fiber is empty. Then $H(x,\cdot)$ is the convex
conjugate of $\ell(x,\cdot)$; when $\ell(x,\cdot)$ is proper, lower
semicontinuous and convex, Fenchel--Moreau gives
$\ell(x,\xi)=\sup_p\{p\cdot\xi-H(x,p)\}$
(Clason, Theorem 5.1(iii), recorded here as source-only orientation;
[[def-legendre-transform-of-a-hamiltonian]] fixes the conjugate notation but
does not prove this extended-valued result). If comparison holds in the
chosen solution class, the viscosity solution is unique.

The sign convention is the one of this page: velocities are integrated forward
from time $0$ to time $t$, the running cost is accumulated forward, the
initial cost is paid at time $0$, and $H$ is convex in $p$ because it is a
supremum of affine functions of $p$, irrespective of convexity of the
control or velocity set. With this convention the
Hopf--Lax operator of [[def-hopf-lax-operator]] is the special case of the
formula in which the infimum over paths has been reduced to a single infimum
over the starting point, $u(x,t)=\inf_y\{u_0(y)+tL((x-y)/t)\}$, for the
autonomous convex superlinear case.

This remark records the interpretation only: no admissible-control framework,
no measurable selection, no existence of optimal controls and no dynamic
programming theorem for control systems is developed on this page, The stationary specialization of the displayed evolution equation is
$H(x,Du)=0$; a separately discounted formulation leads to equations such as
$\lambda u+H(x,Du)=f$. The only dynamic-programming content of
this page is the semigroup law for the Hopf--Lax operator
[[thm-hopf-lax-dynamic-programming-semigroup]], which is proved directly from
the convexity of the Lagrangian. No choice principle is used; this orientation
is recorded so that the Cauchy problems of
[[def-hamilton-jacobi-cauchy-problem]] can be read against their control
origin.
items.strategy: Remark only; no proof. The dictionary between the value function and the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation is stated with the sign conventions fixed by the page: velocities are integrated forward from time $0$ to $t$, costs are nonnegative running costs plus a terminal cost at the initial time, and the Hamiltonian is the Legendre transform $\sup_v\{p\cdot b(x,v)-L(x,v)\}$ of the Lagrangian in the velocity. The remark deliberately excludes the control-theoretic machinery (admissible controls, measurable selection, dynamic programming for control systems); the only dynamic-programming content of the page is the semigroup law for the Hopf--Lax operator [[thm-hopf-lax-dynamic-programming-semigroup]], which is proved directly. This is the orientation permitted by the design; the substantive control theory is out of scope. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Sections 1--3, printed pp. 53--60; [BHJ] Sections 9--10, printed pp. 49--63.

items.title: The eikonal equation as a viscosity equation at a tip
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ and consider the eikonal equation $|Du|=1$ on $\mathbb R^n$, i.e. the first-order equation
$u_t+H(Du)=0$ with $H(p)=|p|-1$ read on functions independent of $t$. The
Euclidean norm $u(x)=|x|$ is a classical solution on
$\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and at its tip $a=0$ it exhibits the difference between the
subsolution inequality $|D\phi|\le1$ and the reverse supersolution inequality
$|D\phi|\ge1$. There is no $C^1$ test function $\phi$ with $u-\phi$ having a
local maximum at $0$: such a contact would force $\phi(x)\ge\phi(0)+|x|$ near
$0$, hence $\langle D\phi(0),h\rangle\ge|h|$ for every direction $h$, which is
impossible for a linear functional. Writing $x_0$ for the coordinate indexed by $0<n$, the $C^1$ functions
$\phi(x)=\varepsilon x_0$ with $0<\varepsilon<1$ satisfy $\phi\le|x|$ near $0$
with equality at $0$, so $u-\phi$ has a local minimum at $0$ and the
supersolution test would require $|D\phi(0)|=\varepsilon\ge1$, which fails.
Hence $u$ is a subsolution of $|Du|=1$ but not a supersolution at the tip: it
satisfies the viscosity subsolution inequality $|Du|\le1$ at the tip and is a viscosity solution of
$|Du|=1$ on $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$.
items.strategy: Verification. Away from the tip $|Du|=1$ holds classically, so the equation is satisfied there by the classical-consistency proposition [[prop-classical-solutions-are-viscosity-solutions]]. Upper contacts at $0$: if $|x|-\phi(x)$ had a local maximum at $0$ with $\phi\in C^1$ and $\phi(0)=0$, then $\phi(x)\ge|x|$ near $0$, so $\langle D\phi(0),h\rangle\ge|h|$ for every direction $h$; testing $h$ and $-h$ gives both $\langle D\phi(0),h\rangle\ge|h|$ and $-\langle D\phi(0),h\rangle\ge|h|$, an impossibility. So there is no upper contact and the subsolution inequality $|D\phi(0)|\le1$ holds vacuously; equivalently the superjet $D^+u(0)$ is empty (a linear form cannot dominate the norm). Lower contacts: for $\phi(x)=\varepsilon x_0$ with $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $x_0$ the coordinate indexed by $0<n$ one has $\phi(x)=\varepsilon x_1\le|x|$ near $0$ with equality at $0$, so $|x|-\phi$ has a local minimum at $0$, and the supersolution test would require $|D\phi(0)|=\varepsilon\ge1$, which fails; this single contact already shows that $u$ is not a supersolution at the tip, hence not a viscosity solution of $|Du|=1$ on any neighbourhood of $0$. The two inequalities are thus genuinely different conditions, and the direction of the cone decides which one the tip satisfies; the check is a computation with the test-function definition and [[lem-viscosity-testing-by-first-order-jets]] and needs no compactness. S: [TR] Chapter 1 Exercise 6 and Exercise 8, printed pp. 19 and 22; [BHJ] Section 3, the eikonal example at a ridge, printed pp. 10--12; [CIL] the discussion of the eikonal equation in Section 1, printed pp. 6--8.

items.title: The quadratic Hopf--Lax formula as an infimal convolution
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ and $H(p)=\tfrac12|p|^2$. Its Legendre transform is
$L(v)=\tfrac12|v|^2$. For every bounded uniformly continuous
$u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, the Hopf--Lax operator of
[[def-hopf-lax-operator]] is, for $t>0$,
$$Q_tu_0(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\Bigl\{u_0(y)+\frac{|x-y|^2}{2t}\Bigr\},$$
the infimal convolution with the quadratic kernel $q_t(z)=|z|^2/(2t)$. The
infimum is attained, and for every minimiser $y$ the Euler relation
$Du_0(y)=(x-y)/t$ holds whenever $u_0$ is differentiable at $y$
([[lem-hopf-lax-minimiser-satisfies-the-characteristic-euler-relation-at-differentiability-points]]).
Separately, the quadratic datum $w_0(y)=\tfrac12|y|^2$ is unbounded and so is
outside the datum class in [[def-hopf-lax-operator]]. Its algebraic infimal
convolution
$$I_t(x):=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\Bigl\{\tfrac12|y|^2+\frac{|x-y|^2}{2t}\Bigr\}$$
has the unique minimiser $y=x/(1+t)$ and value $I_t(x)=|x|^2/(2(1+t))$; this
separate calculation is the Moreau envelope of the quadratic function and does
not apply the bounded-data Hopf--Lax theorem to $w_0$.
items.strategy: For fixed $v$, complete the square in $p$: $p\cdot v-\tfrac12|p|^2=\tfrac12|v|^2-\tfrac12|p-v|^2$, so the supremum is attained at $p=v$ and $L(v)=\tfrac12|v|^2$. For bounded uniformly continuous $u_0$, substituting this Lagrangian in the definition of $Q_t$ gives the displayed infimal convolution. The infimum is attained by [[lem-hopf-lax-infima-localise]], and the conditional Euler relation is [[lem-hopf-lax-minimiser-satisfies-the-characteristic-euler-relation-at-differentiability-points]]. These claims use the stated bounded-data hypotheses. Separately, for $w_0(y)=|y|^2/2$, define $I_t$ directly by the displayed algebraic infimum; no Hopf--Lax theorem or bounded-data attainment lemma is invoked. For $t>0$, $$\frac12|y|^2+\frac{|x-y|^2}{2t}=\frac{1+t}{2t}\left|y-\frac{x}{1+t}\right|^2+\frac{|x|^2}{2(1+t)}.$$ Since the square coefficient is positive, the unique minimiser is $y=x/(1+t)$ and the infimum is $|x|^2/(2(1+t))$. This direct calculation makes no assertion that the unbounded datum lies in the domain of the BUC operator. P: compute the quadratic conjugate, use the in-class Hopf--Lax suppliers only for BUC data, and evaluate the separate quadratic infimum by completing the square. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Example 2.4 and Exercise 22, printed pp. 63 and 68; [BHJ] Section 2, quadratic Lagrangians and infimal convolution, printed pp. 6--9; [CIL] Section 1, the infimal-convolution form, printed pp. 6--8.

items.title: A Hopf--Lax solution with a forming corner from smooth data
items.statement:
Let $H(p)=p^2/2$, $L(v)=v^2/2$, and $u_0(x)=e^{-x^2}-1$. Then $u_0$ is
smooth, bounded and uniformly continuous, with
$p_0(y):=u_0'(y)=-2ye^{-y^2}$ and $u_0''(y)=(4y^2-2)e^{-y^2}$. The
characteristic projection is $X_t(y)=y+tp_0(y)=y-2tye^{-y^2}$, and its lifted
value is $Z_t(y)=u_0(y)+\tfrac t2p_0(y)^2$. For $0\le t<\tfrac12$, $X_t$ is a
diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R$, and $u_{\rm cl}(X_t(y),t)=Z_t(y)$ is the
classical characteristic solution. At $t=\tfrac12$, $X_t'(0)=0$; for
$t>\tfrac12$, putting $s_t=\sqrt{\log(2t)}$ gives
$X_t(-s_t)=X_t(0)=X_t(s_t)=0$, so the characteristic projection is no longer
injective and its single-valued classical graph breaks down. The Hopf--Lax
formula
$$u(x,t)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R}\left\{e^{-y^2}-1+\frac{|x-y|^2}{2t}\right\},\qquad t>0,$$
is finite, satisfies $-1\le u(x,t)\le0$, is uniformly continuous in $x$, and is
a viscosity solution of $u_t+\tfrac12u_x^2=0$ with initial datum $u_0$
([[thm-hopf-lax-formula-solves-the-hamilton-jacobi-equation]],
[[cor-hopf-lax-preserves-a-modulus-of-continuity]]). For each fixed
$t>\tfrac12$, the minimisers at $x=0$ are exactly $y=\pm s_t$, and
$$u(0,t)=\frac{1+\log(2t)}{2t}-1.$$
For $x>0$ sufficiently close to $0$, the unique minimiser tends to $s_t$ as
$x\downarrow0$; for $x<0$ sufficiently close to $0$, it tends to $-s_t$ as
$x\uparrow0$. Thus the one-sided spatial derivatives tend to $-s_t/t$ from the
right and $s_t/t$ from the left, so $u(\cdot,t)$ is continuous but has a corner
at $x=0$.
items.strategy: Verification. Write \(p_0=u_0'\). The characteristic equations for \(H(p)=p^2/2\) give constant momentum \(p_0(y)\), \(X_t(y)=y+tp_0(y)\), and \(Z_t(y)=u_0(y)+tp_0(y)^2/2\). Since \(X_t'(y)=1+t u_0''(y)=1-2te^{-y^2}+4ty^2e^{-y^2}\ge1-2t>0\) for \(t<1/2\), and \(X_t(y)-y\to0\) at both ends of the line, \(X_t\) is a global diffeomorphism. Differentiation of \(Z_t\circ X_t^{-1}\) gives \(u_x=p_0(y)\) and \(u_t=-p_0(y)^2/2\), so this is the classical solution up to the first singular characteristic time. At \(t=1/2\), \(X_t'(0)=0\). For \(t>1/2\), \(s=\sqrt{\log(2t)}>0\) satisfies \(X_t(-s)=X_t(0)=X_t(s)=0\); this proves global noninjectivity. It does not assert local noninjectivity near \(y=0\), where \(X_t'(0)<0\) and the map is locally decreasing. The Hopf--Lax minimum is attained by [[lem-hopf-lax-infima-localise]], and \(-1\le u\le0\) follows from \(u_0\ge-1\), nonnegativity of the cost, and the competitor \(y=x\). The modulus estimate in [[cor-hopf-lax-preserves-a-modulus-of-continuity]] gives spatial uniform continuity; the viscosity-solution clause (not a uniqueness claim) of [[thm-hopf-lax-formula-solves-the-hamilton-jacobi-equation]] applies to this convex superlinear \(H\) and bounded uniformly continuous datum. For the corner, set \(g_t(y)=e^{-y^2}-1+y^2/(2t)\). Its derivative is \(y(1/t-2e^{-y^2})\), so for \(t>1/2\) its critical points are \(0,\pm s\); \(g_t''(0)=1/t-2<0\) and \(g_t''(\pm s)=2s^2/t>0\). Since \(g_t(y)\to\infty\) and \(g_t(\pm s)=-1+(1+\log(2t))/(2t)<0=g_t(0)\), using \(\log r<r-1\) for \(r=2t>1\), its global minimisers are exactly \(\pm s\). For \(G_t(x,y)=u_0(y)+(x-y)^2/(2t)\), any minimiser obeys \(|x-y|\le\sqrt{2t}\), so minimisers for \(x\to0\) are precompact and every cluster point is one of \(\pm s\). Since \(G_t(x,y)-G_t(x,-y)=-2xy/t\), a minimiser cannot be negative when \(x>0\) or positive when \(x<0\); also \(y=0\) is not a minimiser for \(x\ne0\), because \(\partial_yG_t(x,0)=-x/t\ne0\). Thus all minimisers have the sign of \(x\), and as \(x\to0\) they converge to \(s\) from the right and \(-s\) from the left. The stationarity equation is \(x=F_t(y):=y-2tye^{-y^2}\), with \(F_t'(\pm s)=2s^2>0\). The inverse function theorem gives a unique smooth minimising branch on each punctured side near \(x=0\). Along it the envelope derivative is \(u_x=(x-y(x))/t\), so its right and left limits are \(-s/t\) and \(s/t\), respectively. These unequal finite limits give the asserted corner. P: explicit characteristic and minimiser calculations. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Example 2.4 and Section 5.4, printed pp. 67--68; [BHJ] Section 1, characteristic crossing and caustics, printed pp. 2--6; [CIL] Section 1, viscosity solutions through characteristic crossings, printed pp. 6--8.

items.title: The negative absolute value solves the eikonal equation in the viscosity sense
items.statement:
Let $u(x)=-|x|$ on $\mathbb R$. Then $|u'|=1$ for $x\ne0$, and $u$ is a
viscosity solution of the stationary eikonal equation $|u'|-1=0$.
Equivalently, for any $T>0$ its evolutionary extension
$U(x,t):=-|x|-t$ is a viscosity solution of $U_t+|U_x|=0$ on
$\mathbb R\times(0,T)$ ([[def-viscosity-subsolution-and-supersolution]]). At
every point $x\ne0$ the equation holds classically. At the cusp
$(0,t_0)$, every $C^1$ upper test has $\phi_t(0,t_0)=-1$ and satisfies
$|\phi_x(0,t_0)|\le1$, so the subsolution inequality holds, and there is no
$C^1$ test function for which $U-\phi$ has a local minimum at $(0,t_0)$; hence
the supersolution test is vacuous. This is the complementary cusp to
[[ex-eikonal-equation-as-a-viscosity-equation]], where the positive absolute
value fails the supersolution test because it has lower tests with slopes of
modulus less than one.
items.strategy: Away from $x=0$, $U_t=-1$ and $|U_x|=1$, so the classical equation holds; applying [[prop-classical-solutions-are-viscosity-solutions]] on the open set $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ gives the viscosity inequalities there. Fix $(0,t_0)$ and a $C^1$ test $\phi$ with $U(0,t_0)=\phi(0,t_0)$. For either a local maximum or a local minimum of $U-\phi$, restriction to the time line $x=0$ and Fermat's theorem give $-1-\phi_t(0,t_0)=0$, hence $\phi_t(0,t_0)=-1$. Put $p=\phi_x(0,t_0)$. If $U-\phi$ has a local maximum, then at $t=t_0$, $-|x|\le \phi(x,t_0)-\phi(0,t_0)=px+o(|x|)$. Taking $x=h>0$ and $x=-h$ and dividing by $h\downarrow0$ gives $-1\le p\le1$. Thus $\phi_t+|\phi_x|=-1+|p|\le0$, as required for a subsolution. If $U-\phi$ had a local minimum, the inequality instead would be $px+o(|x|)=\phi(x,t_0)-\phi(0,t_0)\le-|x|$. For $x=h>0$ this forces $p\le-1$, while for $x=-h$ it forces $p\ge1$, a contradiction. Thus no lower-contact test exists and the supersolution condition holds vacuously. The contact signs are opposite: upper contacts give $p\in[-1,1]$, whereas a lower contact would require a linear function to lie below $-|x|$ to first order, which is impossible. The positive cusp in [[ex-eikonal-equation-as-a-viscosity-equation]] has the complementary lower tests and therefore fails the supersolution inequality. S: [TR] Chapter 1 Exercise 6 and the discussion of nonsmooth viscosity solutions, printed pp. 19--21; [BHJ] Section 3, examples of viscosity solutions at cusps, printed pp. 10--12.

items.title: Vanishing viscosity selects the Hopf--Lax solution for bounded data
items.statement:
Let $u_0(x)=\sin x$ on $\mathbb R$, a bounded uniformly continuous datum, and
let $H(p)=p^2/2$. For $\varepsilon>0$ and $t>0$ define
$$u^\varepsilon(x,t)=-2\varepsilon\log\!\left[(4\pi\varepsilon t)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\sin y+(x-y)^2/(2t)}{2\varepsilon}\right)\,dy\right],$$
and set $u^\varepsilon(x,0)=\sin x$. Then $u^\varepsilon$ is a bounded classical
solution for $t>0$ of
$$u_t^\varepsilon+\tfrac12|u_x^\varepsilon|^2=\varepsilon u_{xx}^\varepsilon,$$
and it attains $u_0$ uniformly as $t\downarrow0$. The Hopf--Lax function
$$Q_tu_0(x):=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R}\Bigl\{\sin y+\frac{(x-y)^2}{2t}\Bigr\},\qquad Q_0u_0=u_0,$$
is a bounded uniformly continuous viscosity solution of
$u_t+\tfrac12|u_x|^2=0$ with initial trace $u_0$, and for every $T<\infty$ one
has
$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb R,\ 0\le t\le T}|u^\varepsilon(x,t)-Q_tu_0(x)|\le\max\left\{\varepsilon\log(1+T),\ 2\varepsilon\log\left(\sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi\varepsilon}}+\sqrt2\right)\right\}.$$
Both terms on the right tend to zero as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Thus the
viscous solutions converge uniformly on every finite time strip. The estimate
permits an $O(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|)$ error and does not assert a
uniform $O(\varepsilon)$ rate.
items.strategy: Legendre duality gives $L(v)=\sup_p(pv-p^2/2)=v^2/2$ by completing the square, so the displayed $Q_t$ is the Hopf-Lax operator for this Hamiltonian. Write $\Gamma(z,s)=(4\pi s)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/(4s)}$ and $W^\varepsilon(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R}\Gamma(x-y,\varepsilon t)e^{-\sin y/(2\varepsilon)}dy$. The one-dimensional Gaussian integral and the substitution $z=2\sqrt{\varepsilon t}\,r$ give unit mass; the same substitution and the integrable Gaussian tail show that these kernels form an approximate identity. Differentiating the explicit kernel for $t>0$ gives $\partial_t\Gamma(\cdot,\varepsilon t)=\varepsilon\partial_{xx}\Gamma(\cdot,\varepsilon t)$; differentiation under the integral is justified on every compact positive-time interval by a polynomial-times-Gaussian integrable majorant. Hence $W_t^\varepsilon=\varepsilon W_{xx}^\varepsilon$, $W^\varepsilon>0$, and $u^\varepsilon=-2\varepsilon\log W^\varepsilon$ satisfies the viscous equation by direct differentiation. The approximate-identity estimate for the bounded uniformly continuous function $e^{-\sin(\cdot)/(2\varepsilon)}$, which is bounded below by $e^{-1/(2\varepsilon)}$, gives the uniform initial trace after taking the logarithm; averaging also gives $-1\le u^\varepsilon\le1$. For the limit, set $g_{x,t}(y)=\sin y+(x-y)^2/(2t)$ and let $m=Q_tu_0(x)$; a minimizer exists because $g_{x,t}$ is continuous and coercive. Since $g'_{x,t}(y_*)=0$ and $g''_{x,t}(y)=1/t-\sin y\le1+1/t$, Taylor's formula gives $g_{x,t}(y_*+r)\le m+(1+1/t)r^2/2$. Integrating over $|r|\le\sqrt{\varepsilon/(1+1/t)}$ in the Cole-Hopf integral, and using its unit-mass upper bound, yields $$e^{-m/(2\varepsilon)}\frac{e^{-1/4}}{\sqrt{\pi(1+t)}}\le W^\varepsilon(x,t)\le e^{-m/(2\varepsilon)},$$ hence $0\le u^\varepsilon(x,t)-Q_tu_0(x)\le\varepsilon(1/2+\log(\pi(1+t)))$, uniformly in $x$. At $t=0$ both are $u_0$. Also $u_0(x)-t/2\le Q_tu_0(x)\le u_0(x)$ by the 1-Lipschitz bound for sine, so $Q_tu_0$ has the required initial trace and is bounded and uniformly continuous. To verify its viscosity inequalities, use the ready Hopf-Lax dynamic-programming identity $Q_tu_0=Q_h(Q_{t-h}u_0)$: if a $C^1$ function $\phi$ touches $Q$ from above at $(x,t)$, test the infimum with $z=x-h\phi_x(x,t)$, use $Q\le\phi$ nearby, divide the resulting inequality by $h$ and let $h\downarrow0$ to obtain $\phi_t+|\phi_x|^2/2\le0$. If $\phi$ touches $Q$ from below, choose a minimizer $y_*$ in the defining Hopf-Lax formula; the smooth function $F(x,t)=\sin y_*+(x-y_*)^2/(2t)$ satisfies $F\ge Q\ge\phi$ near the contact and equality there, so their first derivatives agree and $\phi_t+|\phi_x|^2/2=F_t+|F_x|^2/2=0$. This proves the supersolution inequality. No global momentum-Lipschitz hypothesis or general vanishing-viscosity theorem is used, and no uniqueness claim is needed.

items.title: Nonconvexity can break the equation; nonsuperlinearity can limit the Lagrangian domain
items.statement:
**False claim:** the Hopf--Lax formula of [[def-hopf-lax-operator]] solves the
equation for every finite superlinear Hamiltonian, and the Legendre transform
of a finite Hamiltonian is real-valued on all of $\mathbb R^n$.

Two separate scope boundaries occur. (a) Convexity is essential if the
Hopf--Lax formula is claimed to solve the equation for the original
Hamiltonian: for $H(p)=p^2-2|p|$ on $\mathbb R$, which is finite and
superlinear but not convex, the formula applied to $u_0\equiv0$ produces
$u(x,t)=t$, and at every interior point the smooth function itself is an upper
test whose residual $u_t+H(u_x)=1+H(0)=1>0$ violates the viscosity subsolution
inequality ([[def-viscosity-subsolution-and-supersolution]]). (b)
Superlinearity is needed for the full-domain real-valued Lagrangian
conclusion: for the finite convex Hamiltonian $H(p)=\sqrt{1+p^2}$, which is
not superlinear, the Legendre transform equals $-\sqrt{1-v^2}$ for
$|v|\le1$ and $+\infty$ for $|v|>1$, so finite action is available only when
$|x-y|\le t$; this is exactly the full-domain finiteness conclusion of
[[lem-hopf-lax-infima-localise]] that fails without superlinearity. The second
clause does not show failure of the value or the solution property: for
$u_0\equiv0$ the formula is $Q_tu_0\equiv-t$, whose residual is
$-1+H(0)=0$.
items.strategy: Refutation and scope calculation. (a) Split the conjugate supremum for $H(p)=p^2-2|p|$ into $p\ge0$ and $p\le0$. On the first half-line, $pv-H(p)=(v+2)p-p^2$, whose supremum is $(v+2)_+^2/4$; on the second, putting $q=-p\ge0$ gives $(2-v)q-q^2$, whose supremum is $(2-v)_+^2/4$. Hence $L(v)$ is their maximum. For $|v|\le2$ this is $(2+|v|)^2/4\ge1$, while for $v\ge2$ the first term is at least $4$ and for $v\le-2$ the second is at least $4$; equality $L(0)=1$ shows $\inf_v L(v)=1$. Since all velocities are available, the formula for $u_0=0$ is $t\inf_vL(v)=t$. At an interior point, the test function $\phi(x,t)=t$ touches $u(x,t)=t$ from above and below. The upper-contact residual is $\phi_t+H(\phi_x)=1+H(0)=1>0$, contradicting the subsolution condition in [[def-viscosity-subsolution-and-supersolution]]; hence the Hopf–Lax output is not a viscosity solution. (b) For $|v|<1$, differentiating $pv-\sqrt{1+p^2}$ gives the maximizer $p=v/\sqrt{1-v^2}$ and value $-\sqrt{1-v^2}$. At $v=\pm1$ the supremum is $0$, approached along the corresponding infinite tail; for $|v|>1$, the expression tends to $+\infty$ along $p=\operatorname{sgn}(v)r$, $r\to\infty$. Thus the stated conjugate and finite domain follow. Its minimum is $-1$ at $v=0$, so for constant datum the formula is $-t$ and has residual zero. The second clause therefore records failure of full-domain real-valuedness, not failure of attainment, localisation, or the PDE solution property. S: [TR] Chapter 2 Section 5.5 and Exercises 22–23, printed pp. 63 and 68–70; [CIL] Section 1, the hypotheses of the Hopf–Lax construction, printed pp. 6–8.

items.title: A strict subsolution can fail the supersolution lower-test condition
items.statement:
**False claim:** for a first-order equation $u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$, passing the
subsolution test at every upper contact forces the supersolution test at every
lower contact, so that a viscosity subsolution which is differentiable is
automatically a viscosity solution.

The claim fails for the equation $u_t+H(u_x)=0$ on
$U=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$ with $H(p)=p$
([[def-viscosity-subsolution-and-supersolution]]): the function
$u(x,t)=-t$ is a viscosity subsolution but not a viscosity supersolution. The
numerical residual $u_t+H(u_x)=-1$ is the same at upper and lower contacts;
what differs is the direction of the inequality that the definition requires.
items.strategy: Refutation by direct test. By [[def-viscosity-subsolution-and-supersolution]], subsolutions are tested at local maxima of \(u-\phi\) with the inequality \(\phi_t+\phi_x\le0\), while supersolutions are tested at local minima with \(\phi_t+\phi_x\ge0\). For \(u(x,t)=-t\), an upper contact has \(u-\phi\) locally maximal; since \(u-\phi\) is differentiable, [[thm-fermat-for-euclidean-local-extrema]] gives \(D\phi=Du=(0,-1)\), and hence residual \(-1\le0\) at every upper test. Thus \(u\) is a viscosity subsolution. For the supersolution test choose \(\phi=u\); then \(u-\phi\equiv0\) has a local minimum, but the residual is \(-1<0\), so the lower-test supersolution inequality fails. The example distinguishes the two required contact inequalities without claiming that the residual itself changes with contact direction. S: [TR] Chapter 1 Exercise 7, printed p. 19; [BHJ] Section 3, elementary sign checks, printed pp. 10--12.

items.title: Minima of viscosity subsolutions need not be subsolutions
items.statement:
**False claim:** a finite minimum of finitely many viscosity subsolutions of a
first-order equation is again a viscosity subsolution.

Take the stationary proper equation
$$F(x,u,u'):=u+1-(u')^2=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega=(-1,1),$$
whose operator $F(r,p)=r+1-p^2$ is continuous and strictly increasing in $r$
(proper), and the two affine functions $u_1(x)=1-2x$ and $u_2(x)=1+2x$. Both
are classical subsolutions: $F(u_i,u_i')=u_i+1-4=u_i-3\le0$ on $\Omega$
because $u_i\le3$ there. Their pointwise minimum is $u(x)=1-2|x|$, a peak at
$x_0=0$ with value $1$. The $C^1$ test function $\phi\equiv1$ satisfies
$\phi\ge u$ on $\Omega$ with equality at $0$, so $u-\phi$ has a local maximum
at $0$; but $F(0,u(0),\phi'(0))=1+1-0=2>0$, so $u$ fails the subsolution test
at the corner. Hence the finite-minimum operation is not admissible for
subsolutions of a proper equation, while the finite maximum of subsolutions and
the finite minimum of supersolutions are, by the same active-index contact
argument as [[prop-maxima-of-subsolutions-and-minima-of-supersolutions]]:
the active function has the same value and the same test at the contact. The zero-order term contributes to this residual but is not essential to
failure of the minimum operation: for $F(p)=1-p^2$ the same two affine
functions have residual $-3$, while their minimum has the upper-test
residual $F(0)=1>0$.
items.strategy: Refutation by explicit touching test. The two affine functions are classical subsolutions because $F(u_i,u_i')=u_i-3\le0$ pointwise on $\Omega$; being $C^1$ classical subsolutions of a first-order equation, they are viscosity subsolutions in the test-function sense (the definition is the evident adaptation of [[def-viscosity-subsolution-and-supersolution]] to a proper operator $F(x,r,p)$: the inequality $F(x_0,u(x_0),D\phi(x_0))\le0$ is required at every local maximum of $u-\phi$). Their pointwise minimum is $u=1-2|x|$, and $\phi\equiv1$ is $C^1$ with $\phi\ge u$ on $\Omega$ and equality exactly at $0$, so $u-\phi$ has a local maximum at $0$; the subsolution inequality would require $F(0,1,0)=1+1-0\le0$, which is false. The zero-order term $u$ is what makes the corner value $u(0)=1$ enter with the wrong sign, while the two affine functions themselves have values at most $3$ and slopes $\mp2$ with $-p^2$ terms that more than compensate: this is exactly why a proper equation can fail the mixed operation and why the maximum/minimum proposition of [[prop-maxima-of-subsolutions-and-minima-of-supersolutions]] is stated for the specific Hamilton--Jacobi operator $u_t+H(x,t,Du)$ with no zero-order term. Every step is an explicit computation of the two quadratic expressions. S: [CIL] the discussion of properness and of finite infima of supersolutions in Section 4 and Section 5, printed pp. 22--25 and 35--36; [TR] Chapter 1 Section 8, the discussion following Lemma 1.25, printed p. 33.

items.title: The eikonal equation on an interval has many solutions when endpoint data are omitted
items.statement:
**False claim:** the stationary eikonal equation $|u'|=1$ on $\Omega=(0,1)$ has
a unique viscosity solution when no boundary data are prescribed.

The functions $u_1(x)=x$, $u_2(x)=1-x$ and
$u_3(x)=\tfrac12-|x-\tfrac12|=\min\{x,1-x\}$ are viscosity solutions of
$|u'|=1$ on $(0,1)$
([[def-viscosity-subsolution-and-supersolution]],
[[lem-viscosity-testing-by-first-order-jets]]). They are pairwise distinct, and
their continuous boundary traces are respectively $(0,1)$, $(1,0)$ and
$(0,0)$; in particular the equation without prescribed endpoint data does not
select a unique solution, and the examples are distinguished by their boundary
traces.
items.strategy: Write $F(p)=|p|-1$ and lift each stationary profile to $U_i(x,t)=u_i(x)$ for the equation $U_t+F(U_x)=0$. At a contact with a $C^1$ test in space-time, the time derivative of the test is zero because $U_i$ is independent of time. Away from $x_0=1/2$, each profile is $C^1$ and has spatial derivative $1$ or $-1$, so both viscosity inequalities hold. At $x_0$, write $h=x-x_0$ and $u_3(x_0+h)=1/2-|h|$. If $\phi$ is an upper test with $p=\phi'(x_0)$, normalize $\phi(x_0)=1/2$ and use $\phi(x_0+h)=1/2+ph+o(|h|)$. The inequality $u_3\le\phi$ for $h>0$ gives $p\ge-1$, while for $h<0$ it gives $p\le1$. Hence every upper-test slope lies in $[-1,1]$ and $F(p)\le0$. If $\phi$ were a lower test, $u_3\ge\phi$ for $h>0$ would give $p\le-1$, while for $h<0$ it would give $p\ge1$; these conditions are incompatible, so no lower test exists and the supersolution condition is vacuous. For pairwise distinctness, at $x=1/4$ one has $(u_1,u_2,u_3)=(1/4,3/4,1/4)$, and at $x=3/4$ one has $(u_1,u_2,u_3)=(3/4,1/4,1/4)$; these values distinguish every pair. Also $u_1-u_2=2x-1$ changes sign. Evaluating the continuous extensions at the endpoints gives traces $(0,1)$, $(1,0)$, and $(0,0)$. Thus omitted boundary data leave multiple solutions, while the displayed candidates have different endpoint traces. P: direct test-function verification at the peak and explicit boundary evaluation.

items.title: Distance to the boundary solves the unit eikonal Dirichlet problem on the ball
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $\Omega=B(0,1)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be the open unit ball and let
$d(x):=1-|x|=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$. Then $d$ is Lipschitz with
$|Dd|=1$ at every $x\ne0$, continuous on $\overline\Omega$ with $d=0$ on
$\partial\Omega$, and $d$ is a viscosity solution of the stationary eikonal
equation with zero boundary data:
$$|Du|=1\ \text{in }\Omega,\qquad u=0\ \text{on }\partial\Omega .$$
At $x\ne0$ the equation holds classically; at the centre the function has a
peak, every $C^1$ test function $\phi$ with $d-\phi$ having a local maximum at
$0$ satisfies $|D\phi(0)|\le1$ (the subsolution inequality), and no $C^1$
test function has $d-\phi$ locally minimal at $0$: a lower contact would require
$\langle D\phi(0),h\rangle\le-|h|$ for all $h$, which is impossible, so no such
contact exists and the supersolution test is vacuous at the centre. Hence $d$
is a viscosity solution. The example is the canonical nonsmooth

items.strategy: Verification. For $x\ne0$, $d$ is smooth with $Dd(x)=-x/|x|$, so $|Dd(x)|=1$ and the equation holds classically. At $x=0$: if $d-\phi$ has a local maximum at $0$ with $\phi(0)=1$, then $1-|x|\le\phi(x)\le\phi(0)+\langle D\phi(0),x\rangle+o(|x|)=1+\langle D\phi(0),x\rangle+o(|x|)$, so $\langle D\phi(0),x\rangle\ge-|x|+o(|x|)$; replacing $x$ by $-x$ gives $|\langle D\phi(0),x\rangle|\le|x|$ and hence $|D\phi(0)|\le1$, which is the subsolution inequality. If $d-\phi$ had a local minimum at $0$, then $1-|x|\ge 1+\langle D\phi(0),x\rangle+o(|x|)$, i.e. $\langle D\phi(0),x\rangle\le-|x|+o(|x|)$, and testing $x$ and $-x$ forces the impossible $\langle D\phi(0),x\rangle=-|x|$ for every $x$ simultaneously; so the set of lower contacts is empty and the supersolution inequality holds vacuously. The boundary values are zero by the definition of $d$. This is exactly the metric triangle inequality in the form $d(x)\le d(y)+|x-y|$ specialised to the ball, and it is the model example of a distance solution with nonsmooth data.
